Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models

Andi Gu Email: andigu@g.harvard.edu Affiliation: Harvard Quantum Initiative for Science and Engineering, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Affiliation: Anthropic STEM Fellows Program    Alek H. Kemeny Affiliation: Anthropic    Susanne F. Yelin Affiliation: Harvard Quantum Initiative for Science and Engineering, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA    Mikhail D. Lukin Affiliation: Harvard Quantum Initiative for Science and Engineering, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Affiliation: QuEra Computing, 1380 Soldiers Field Road, Boston, MA 02135, USA
Abstract

Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps—a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic—viable and substantially improves the Toffoli–qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

Computational primitives based on classical function evaluation play a central role in a wide range of quantum algorithms. Such primitives include decoding routines for optimization [1], numerical functions for quantum simulation [2], arithmetic routines for number theory [3], and quantum read-only memory (QROM), which coherently loads classically specified data into quantum registers [4]. To operate on quantum data, these functions must be compiled into circuits that can be executed coherently on quantum hardware. This imposes two constraints absent from ordinary classical programs. First, because the input may be in superposition, the circuit cannot inspect an intermediate value and select an ordinary classical control-flow path. Data-dependent behavior is instead expressed through controlled operations within a fixed gate sequence, so every branch contributes to the circuit’s cost even if it applies only to some inputs. Second, the computation must be reversible: intermediate information cannot simply be overwritten or discarded. Temporary values must eventually be uncomputed, returning their qubits to their initial state and preventing residual information from remaining entangled with the output. Until they are uncomputed, these values occupy additional qubits. At the same time, when bounded error is permitted, machinery needed only for rare or atypical inputs can sometimes be omitted, reducing resource requirements while keeping the failure probability controlled. Efficient coherent compilation is of major practical importance, and recent reductions in resource requirements have come from coordinated changes to arithmetic algorithms, data representations, and their reversible implementation [5, 6]. Such redesigns are difficult for general quantum circuits because directly testing correctness can require exponentially expensive classical simulation or fully operational large-scale quantum processors. Automated circuit optimizers therefore typically preserve correctness by restricting the search to predefined equivalence-preserving rewrites [7], limiting them to variations of a fixed design.

Here we introduce a framework that pairs large language model (LLM) proposals with an independent evaluator that verifies and scores each candidate. We focus on a class of quantum circuits that compute a classical function ff: for an arbitrary input |ψ⟩=∑x,yαx,y​|x⟩​|y⟩\ket{\psi}=\sum_{x,y}\alpha_{x,y}\ket{x}\ket{y}, the circuit must act as |ψ⟩⟼∑x,yαx,y​|x⟩​|y⊕f⁡(x)⟩\ket{\psi}\longmapsto\sum_{x,y}\alpha_{x,y}\ket{x}\ket{y\oplus f(x)}, where |x⟩\ket{x} and |y⟩\ket{y} are computational-basis states of the input and output registers, respectively. By linearity, this coherent action is correct if the circuit performs the required map on every computational-basis input: |x⟩​|y⟩⟼|x⟩​|y⊕f⁡(x)⟩\ket{x}\ket{y}\longmapsto\ket{x}\ket{y\oplus f(x)}. This basis-state reduction makes candidate circuits amenable to programmatic evaluation, since every allowed operation maps a computational-basis state to another computational-basis state, possibly changing its phase, but never creating a superposition [8]. The action of a candidate on any chosen input can therefore be simulated by tracking a bit string and its phase, rather than 2n2^{n} amplitudes. Resource accounting is also simple: we use the Toffoli count TT and the peak qubit count QQ, and rank circuits by their product, the T​QTQ-cost. Together, these properties let us build an efficient, programmatic evaluator that checks the correctness and resource cost of any candidate circuit design.

Each search begins from a hand-written task specification and a blank program; the specification states the required circuit behavior but provides no implementation guidance. The LLM proposes a candidate and iteratively revises it using evaluator feedback (Figure 1(a)). Previous work represents candidates as sequences of gates or predefined circuit blocks [9, 10], which can obscure the algorithmic structure of the circuit. Our framework instead lets the LLM propose and revise candidates through a high-level Python interface, where reusable functions and ordinary programming constructs make that structure explicit. This allows a single conceptual change to reorganize operations throughout the circuit, while the evaluator tests its consequences for correctness and resource cost. However, purely iterative refinement of a single candidate can remain tied to the architecture from which it began, resulting in convergence to local (but not necessarily global) optima. We therefore start with an ideation stage in which the LLM is prompted to propose several distinct algorithm families, each representing a different approach to the problem. Circuits within each family are optimized independently in parallel, allowing the search to explore different strategies rather than only variations of one design. Well-performing candidates are periodically shared between families so that an idea discovered in one approach can inform another.

Across eight diverse compilation tasks, the discovered circuits repeatedly exhibit three common principles of algorithm–circuit co-design. These principles address the features of coherent compilation described above: expressing data-dependent control flow, making intermediate computations reversible without retaining their entire history, and using a failure budget to remove circuit resources devoted to atypical cases (see Figure 1).

Design principles

One recurring principle in the circuits discovered by the search is to replace conditional arithmetic with conditional routing. A naïve coherent translation of a casewise classical algorithm includes a separately controlled arithmetic block for every branch. The discovered circuits instead use a representation in which the branches differ primarily in which values occupy particular computational roles. Relatively cheap controlled swaps then route the appropriate values into those roles, one unconditional arithmetic path performs the expensive work, and further routing places the results in their required registers. In this sense, where a classical program routes execution to the selected operation, the coherent circuit routes the selected data through a shared operation. The idea resembles bucket-brigade quantum random-access memory (QRAM) [11].

For example, consider four nn-qubit fixed-point registers cc, xx, yy, and zz, together with a control qubit bb. Suppose that we wish to perform

x⟼{x+c​yfor ​b=0,x+c​zfor ​b=1,x\longmapsto\begin{cases}x+cy&\text{for }b=0,\\ x+cz&\text{for }b=1,\end{cases} (1)

while returning cc, yy, and zz unchanged. A naïve implementation uses two controlled multiply-adds. Conditional routing instead swaps yy and zz according to bb, applies one uncontrolled multiply-add, and undoes the swap. For the standard schoolbook construction [12], this reduces the Toffoli count from Tnaive​(n)=3​n2+17​n−2T_{\mathrm{naive}}(n)=3n^{2}+17n-2 to Trouted​(n)=(3​n2+17​n−2)/2T_{\mathrm{routed}}(n)=(3n^{2}+17n-2)/2, as shown in Figure 1(b).

More generally, conditional routing requires canonicalizing branch-dependent states into a representation on which the same expensive computation applies. Schematically, when the branch can be expressed as Ub=Rb−1​K​RbU_{b}=R_{b}^{-1}KR_{b}, the circuit need only control the inexpensive routing transformation RbR_{b}; the expensive kernel KK appears once and need not be controlled. Finding such a decomposition typically takes more than recognizing identical arithmetic in two branches: it exploits an equivalence in the required output so that apparently different updates become instances of the same computation. The difficulty lies less in the routing circuit than in determining which branch-dependent differences matter and which can be absorbed into a shared representation.

Reversibility creates a second challenge: reversing a conditional update requires knowing which branch was taken during the forward computation. A naïve implementation records each decision in a history stack whose size grows with the number of updates. But the branch decisions need not always be stored explicitly: different branches may leave distinguishable patterns in registers that remain available during uncomputation. As illustrated in Figure 1(c), the circuit can recover the branch bit from such a pattern, use it to select the appropriate inverse update, and then clear the recovered bit, so the register contents serve as an inexpensive record of the branch decisions. For example, suppose we have a register gg that begins at g0=0g_{0}=0. In round jj, conditioned on some branch bit bjb_{j}, we add 2j2^{j}, so that

gj+1=gj+bj​2j.g_{j+1}=g_{j}+b_{j}2^{j}. (2)

For arbitrary values of gjg_{j}, there is no way to tell from gj+1g_{j+1} which branch was taken. Globally, however, there is an important invariant: gj<2jg_{j}<2^{j}, and therefore bit jj of gj+1g_{j+1} must equal bjb_{j}. During uncomputation, the circuit can simply read this bit to recover bjb_{j}. The computation’s evolving state thus supplies the branch decisions in reverse order without a separate history stack. In general, finding such a decoder requires the forward algorithm, its data representation, and its uncomputation procedure to be designed together. Viewed locally, an update may be ambiguous, since either branch can appear to admit a valid predecessor. The ambiguity can disappear once the circuit is restricted to states reachable from the prescribed initialization, where a relation across the registers can distinguish histories that no single register can.

The third principle exploits the small but finite failure probability permitted by most quantum algorithms. Turning this failure budget into resource savings, however, is not automatic. One must first identify the rare inputs that determine worst-case resource requirements. Unlike a classical program, a quantum circuit must contain the gates and ancillas required by every supported path. A rare input can therefore determine the circuit’s Toffoli count or peak qubit count. Yet identifying such inputs is not enough: the circuitry supporting them may not be separable from the computation on typical inputs. The co-design task is to reorganize the computation so that the additional resources required by rare inputs are localized—for example, to extra iterations, stack entries, or arithmetic lanes. Those components can then be omitted while confining failure to the low-probability inputs that require them (Figure 1(d)). In what follows we show how these design principles result in significantly improved algorithmic circuits across a wide variety of quantum tasks.

Reversible syndrome decoding for DQI

Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is a quantum algorithm that turns certain optimization problems into decoding problems for classical error-correcting codes, using quantum interference to favor better solutions. A central application is optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), a form of polynomial fitting over finite fields for which DQI offers a superpolynomial speedup over known classical algorithms. DQI achieves this by using a Reed–Solomon decoder as a subroutine within the quantum computation [1]. The decoder identifies the positions and values of errors from a collection of algebraic checks called syndromes. DQI requires this decoding to run coherently on a superposition of inputs, making the reversible decoder a dominant resource cost. Khattar et al. [13] compiled DQI circuits for OPI over binary extension fields using reversible Reed–Solomon decoders based on the extended Euclidean algorithm.

We study their primary Reed–Solomon instance, in which 70 syndrome values uniquely determine an error pattern containing at most 35 errors. Our search framework discovered a circuit that replaces their synchronized Euclidean solve with the Berlekamp–Massey (BM) recurrence. BM substantially reduces the arithmetic cost, but its updates overwrite intermediate values that a naïve reversible implementation would retain in a large history stack. The discovered circuit preserves BM’s arithmetic advantage while avoiding most of this storage (Figure 2).

Reed–Solomon decoding amounts to determining which positions in the data contain errors. The LL error positions are encoded in a locator polynomial σ⁡(z)=∑k=0Lσk​zk\sigma(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{L}\sigma_{k}z^{k}, whose roots identify those positions. To recover the locator coefficients, BM solves for the lowest-degree nonzero polynomial whose convolution (see Figure 2(d)) with the syndrome sequence vanishes:

(S∗σ)r=∑k=0LσkSr−k=0,r=L+1,…,70.(S*\sigma)_{r}=\sum_{k=0}^{L}\sigma_{k}S_{r-k}=0,\qquad r=L+1,\ldots,70. (3)

BM constructs the locator incrementally. At each round, the convolution evaluated at the next syndrome gives the discrepancy Δ\Delta: if it vanishes, no correction is needed; otherwise, BM adjusts the locator coefficients and, when necessary, increases its degree.

To make a correction without invalidating previous rounds of updates, BM retains an earlier polynomial τ\tau as a correction template, together with its nonzero discrepancy δ\delta. When Δ≠0\Delta\neq 0, BM scales τ\tau by α=Δ/δ\alpha=\Delta/\delta and applies the correction σ←σ−α​τ\sigma\leftarrow\sigma-\alpha\tau. BM keeps the template until the current locator has accumulated enough information from subsequent syndromes to take over its role:

(σ−α​τ,τ,δ)\displaystyle(\sigma-\alpha\tau,\tau,\delta) (retain),\displaystyle\quad\text{(retain)}, (4a)
(σ−α​τ,σ,Δ)\displaystyle(\sigma-\alpha\tau,\sigma,\Delta) (replace).\displaystyle\quad\text{(replace)}. (4b)

The replace update in Equation 4b creates the main reversibility problem: it overwrites the previous template τ\tau and discrepancy δ\delta. A naïve reversible implementation stores these displaced values so that the update can later be undone. Over repeated rounds, this accumulates a history of whole polynomials (Figure 2(b)).

The discovered circuit avoids this polynomial history by exploiting a freedom in the decoding task: the locator is needed only up to a nonzero multiplicative factor, because rescaling leaves its roots unchanged. The circuit (Figure 2(c)) therefore implements a rescaled version of both branches of Equation 4, using simple conditional routing and a single shared update:

(σ−α​τ,τ,δ)\displaystyle(\sigma-\alpha\tau,\tau,\delta) (retain),\displaystyle\quad\text{(retain)}, (5a)
(τ−α−1​σ,σ,Δ)\displaystyle(\tau-\alpha^{-1}\sigma,\sigma,\Delta) (replace).\displaystyle\quad\text{(replace)}. (5b)

The result τ−α−1​σ=−α−1​(σ−α​τ)\tau-\alpha^{-1}\sigma=-\alpha^{-1}(\sigma-\alpha\tau) differs from the locator in the unrescaled update only by the nonzero scale factor −α−1-\alpha^{-1} and so has the same roots. Both branches can then use one shared arithmetic path without storing the displaced template τ\tau.

This resolves the history problem for the polynomial registers, but the discrepancies present a second reversibility problem. To uncompute a correction, the circuit must recover whichever discrepancy is no longer present after the update. The replace case of Equation 5b overwrites the stored value δold\delta_{\mathrm{old}} with δnew=Δ\delta_{\mathrm{new}}=\Delta, but the circuit can decode δold\delta_{\mathrm{old}} from the constant coefficients of the updated locator registers. BM shifts the template by one power of zz every round, so τ\tau has zero constant coefficient entering the round. Writing σ0\sigma_{0} and τ0\tau_{0} for the constant coefficients after the update gives δold=σ0​τ0−1​δnew\delta_{\mathrm{old}}=\sigma_{0}\tau_{0}^{-1}\delta_{\mathrm{new}}. This case thus adds no entry to the history stack. In fact, the circuit never stores δ\delta at all: the same relation fixes δ\delta in terms of the locator’s constant coefficient (Supplementary Information [SI] I.1). The retain update of Equation 5a is the exception: it keeps the previous discrepancy δ\delta, while the current discrepancy Δ\Delta, which is needed to reverse the correction, remains only in a temporary register. Each retain update therefore stores Δ\Delta on the history stack. In the worst case, 35 stack entries (665 qubits) would be needed. Under the DQI input distribution, a second stack entry is required with probability 1.0×10−41.0\times 10^{-4}, so the discovered circuit allocates only one stack entry (19 qubits instead of 665) and permits failure on these rare inputs.

Together, these transformations make the arithmetically efficient BM algorithm suitable for reversible computation.

Reversible modular inversion

Modular inversion is the task of finding xx such that w​x≡1(modp)wx\equiv 1\pmod{p}, given a nonzero input ww and a prime pp. It is a central arithmetic subroutine in a range of quantum algorithms [14, 3]. A standard way to compute the inverse is through the extended Euclidean algorithm. Euclidean algorithms repeatedly simplify a pair of integers while preserving their greatest common divisor. By tracking how this divisor is expressed in terms of the original inputs, they also recover coefficients α,β\alpha,\beta satisfying α​p+β​w=1\alpha p+\beta w=1, so β\beta is the inverse of ww modulo pp.

Divsteps is a variant of the Euclidean algorithm that replaces division with conditional additions, subtractions, and halving [15]. Starting from f=pf=p and g=wg=w, the goal is to reduce the pair to f=±1f=\pm 1 and g=0g=0 while preserving their greatest common divisor. The basic strategy is to hold the odd integer ff fixed while reducing gg: if gg is even, it can be halved directly; if gg is odd, adding or subtracting ff first makes it even. These operations preserve the greatest common divisor because ff is odd. Holding ff fixed indefinitely, however, would leave only one integer being reduced, so the algorithm must periodically swap their roles. A small signed counter zz schedules these swaps without ever comparing ff and gg: it roughly tracks how many more bits ff has than gg, so a swap occurs once gg is likely the smaller of the two. This allows both integers to be reduced using only inexpensive arithmetic and control. Two auxiliary integers fvf_{v} and gvg_{v} track the input’s contribution in a scaled form: after tt steps, they satisfy fv​w≡2t​f(modp)f_{v}w\equiv 2^{t}f\pmod{p} and gv​w≡2t​g(modp)g_{v}w\equiv 2^{t}g\pmod{p}. Thus, at termination, f​fvff_{v} gives the desired inverse up to the scaling factor 2t2^{t}. The scaling keeps the coefficient updates free of division. Starting from (z,f,g,fv,gv)=(0,p,w,0,1)(z,f,g,f_{v},g_{v})=(0,p,w,0,1), each step applies one of three updates:

(−z,g,(g−f)/2, 2​gv,gv−fv)\displaystyle(-z,\ g,\ (g-f)/2,\ 2g_{v},\ g_{v}-f_{v}) for ​z≥0,g​ odd,\displaystyle\quad\text{for }z\geq 0,\ g\text{ odd}, (6a)
(z+1,f,(g+f)/2, 2​fv,gv+fv)\displaystyle(z+1,\ f,\ (g+f)/2,\ 2f_{v},\ g_{v}+f_{v}) for ​z<0,g​ odd,\displaystyle\quad\text{for }z<0,\ g\text{ odd}, (6b)
(z+1,f,g/2, 2​fv,gv)\displaystyle(z+1,\ f,\ g/2,\ 2f_{v},\ g_{v}) for ​g​ even.\displaystyle\quad\text{for }g\text{ even}. (6c)

Classically, each update overwrites the current state. Reversing the computation, however, requires knowing which of the three updates was applied. A naïve implementation would store this choice at every step, accumulating a history stack alongside the arithmetic registers. The discovered circuit instead recovers decisions from the current arithmetic state. Some decisions are easy to recover from the updated registers, while others require a more involved decoding procedure. We label each update by two bits: ss records whether the step swaps the roles of ff and gg, and bb records whether the incoming gg is odd. The updates in Equations 6a, 6b and 6c have labels (s,b)=(1,1),(0,1),(0,0)(s,b)=(1,1),(0,1),(0,0), respectively. The task during uncomputation is to recover these bits from the updated state.

For many steps, recovering bb and ss requires only a few observations about the updated registers. A swap (Equation 6a) always leaves a distinctive pattern in fv′f_{v}^{\prime}. To see this, note that throughout the recurrence, fvf_{v} is even and gvg_{v} is odd. A swap sets fv′=2​gvf_{v}^{\prime}=2g_{v}, which has exactly one trailing zero bit, whereas a nonswap sets fv′=2​fvf_{v}^{\prime}=2f_{v}, which is divisible by four. Thus the updated coefficient identifies every swap, recovering both s=1s=1 and b=1b=1; otherwise, s=0s=0, so the swap bit ss is always cheaply recoverable. For nonswaps, two further tests determine bb. If z′≥1z^{\prime}\geq 1, the incoming gg must have been even, since an odd value would have triggered a swap. If the step first reaches g′=0g^{\prime}=0, the incoming gg must instead have been odd, since halving a nonzero even integer cannot give zero. Together, these simple tests recover about two thirds of the decisions in a typical walk (the sequence of divsteps applied to one input). The only unresolved cases are nonterminating nonswaps with z′≤0z^{\prime}\leq 0, where the circuit must determine whether the step added fvf_{v} to gvg_{v}, that is, the bit bb in the update (fv′,gv′)=(2​fv,gv+b​fv)(f_{v}^{\prime},g_{v}^{\prime})=(2f_{v},g_{v}+bf_{v}).

Consider a swap followed by a sequence of these ambiguous nonswaps, which we call an excursion. Immediately after the swap, fv=2​qf_{v}=2q for some odd qq. On the jjth step of the excursion, fv=2j−1​qf_{v}=2^{j-1}q (hence fv′=2j​qf_{v}^{\prime}=2^{j}q), where the excursion depth jj counts the initiating swap as step 1. Equivalently, jj is the number of trailing zero bits in the updated coefficient fv′f_{v}^{\prime}. The update to gvg_{v} becomes

gv′=gv+b​2j−1​q.g_{v}^{\prime}=g_{v}+b2^{j-1}q. (7)

Note that this almost matches the binary-record construction in Equation 2. The only difference is the shared factor qq: to recover bb, we need to remove the factor qq from the update. Since fv′=2j​qf_{v}^{\prime}=2^{j}q is known, we can recover qq by removing the trailing zero bits from fv′f_{v}^{\prime}. To remove the same factor from both sides of the update, we multiply by q−1q^{-1} modulo 2j2^{j}; this inverse exists because qq is odd. The update rule then becomes

gv′​q−1mod2j=(gv​q−1mod2j)+b​2j−1.g_{v}^{\prime}q^{-1}\bmod 2^{j}=(g_{v}q^{-1}\bmod 2^{j})+b2^{j-1}. (8)

Crucially, in Appendix A, we show that (gv​q−1mod2j)<2j−1(g_{v}q^{-1}\bmod 2^{j})<2^{j-1}. Therefore,

b=bitj−1⁡(gv′​q−1mod2j),b=\operatorname{bit}_{j-1}\!\left(g_{v}^{\prime}q^{-1}\bmod 2^{j}\right), (9)

where bit positions are counted from zero at the least significant (rightmost) bit. Every quantity on the right-hand side is determined by the updated registers, so the rule recovers the branch decision without access to the previous state. This recovery relies on a global invariant ensuring that earlier branch history cannot contaminate the deciding bit. The LLM identified this invariant, which links information accumulated across successive updates to the branch decisions needed during uncomputation, and developed it into a proof that the arithmetic state retains the information required for recovery [16].

For a given jj, the rule in Equation 9 depends only on the lowest jj bits of gv′g_{v}^{\prime} and the lowest jj bits of qq. Therefore, for each small value of jj, we treat the decoding rule as a truth table mapping 2​j2j input bits to a single bit bb, and compile it directly into a Boolean circuit. For larger jj, the decoder must inspect more bits and becomes increasingly expensive. Although every decision is recoverable in principle, decoding all of them does not give the cheapest circuit. A tunable cutoff jstorej_{\mathrm{store}} determines which ambiguous decisions are decoded and which are stored. At depths j<jstorej<j_{\mathrm{store}}, the circuit uses a decoder; at depths j≥jstorej\geq j_{\mathrm{store}}, it writes the decision to a history stack. Increasing the cutoff spends more Toffolis on decoding while reducing the required history storage, giving a family of circuits that trade Toffoli count against qubit count (SI II).

Further savings are possible when the application permits a small failure probability. We use this failure budget to exclude rare, unusually demanding inputs through two resource limits: a fixed history-stack size and a fixed window of supported stopping times. The history-stack limit builds on the decoding trade-off. With jstore=5j_{\mathrm{store}}=5, only 12.4%12.4\% of ambiguous decisions are written to the stack (Figure 3(a)). On average, the required stack size is 21 history qubits, but it can reach 263 in the worst case. We instead reserve 60 and allow the circuit to fail on rare inputs for which the stack overflows. Such overflows occur with probability 2.4×10−62.4\times 10^{-6} per inversion (Figure 3(b)), saving 203 history qubits relative to the worst case. The stopping-time limit addresses a separate cost. A fixed quantum circuit must schedule enough steps for every input it supports. Although 590 divsteps suffice even in the worst case, stopping times are concentrated in a much narrower range (Figure 3(b)). The discovered circuit therefore schedules 533 steps and tests for termination only from step 499 onward; inputs that terminate outside this window are allowed to fail.

Branch decoding and bounded resource allocation thus make divsteps practical for reversible modular inversion. A complete benchmark circuit built on this inversion (SI II) uses 4.0 million Toffolis and 935 qubits.

Discussion and outlook

The DQI and modular inversion constructions illustrate how redesigning the representation and uncomputation of an algorithm can substantially reduce its quantum resource requirements. Similar gains arise across the other tasks studied here. For seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuit uses both fewer Toffolis and fewer qubits than the corresponding baseline. Table 1 summarizes these improvements, and the Supplementary Information gives details for each task.

A recurring source of these gains is the recovery of classical algorithmic efficiency under the constraints of quantum computation. In a naïve reversible implementation, coherent control and cleanup can introduce enough overhead to obscure the advantages of an efficient classical method. Our Berlekamp–Massey and divstep constructions show how jointly choosing the algorithm, representation, and uncomputation can recover those advantages. These results suggest that some apparent costs of quantum arithmetic reflect limitations of existing reversible constructions rather than of the algorithms themselves.

Finding such constructions requires reasoning about choices whose benefits depend on one another. An arithmetic saving may become useful only after the associated control and uncomputation costs have also been reduced. A candidate design must therefore be carried through several unresolved mathematical and implementation problems before its resource advantage becomes apparent.

The framework is bounded by the choices that define each task. One is the objective that ranks circuits: we use the T​QTQ-cost for a uniform comparison, but other objectives are equally reasonable. In practice, the relative importance of qubit count, depth, routing, and measurements depends on details such as hardware constraints, decoder performance, and error-correction architecture. The scoring function can be replaced with a hardware-appropriate combination of these resources, but determining that objective remains a matter of application and hardware judgment. The circuit interface defines a second boundary. Here, the required transformation is specified in a fixed computational basis, excluding optimizations whose advantage comes from changing the encoding itself. For example, coset representations can make modular addition cheaper by encoding each residue as a superposition of congruent integers, which avoids conventional comparisons and corrections at the cost of an exponentially small error [17, 18], but such encodings lie outside the present framework. More generally, the task boundary, input distribution, data representations, and accuracy target make a search well posed while also encoding assumptions about how the circuit is embedded in a larger algorithm (in particular, which states it receives and how its outputs are consumed).

The same choices that bound the search also make reliable programmatic feedback possible: they specify what each candidate must preserve and which resource trade-offs the evaluator should reward. Within these boundaries, our results show that evaluator-guided LLM search can go beyond refining a fixed circuit to uncover new reversible algorithms and representations. Related approaches have produced new algorithms in combinatorics and linear algebra [19, 20]. These observations suggest a practical criterion for extending the approach: wherever a problem admits a sufficiently expressive task interface and its correctness and resource costs can be evaluated cheaply enough to sustain many rounds of search, the same evaluator-guided search may provide a route to new algorithms.

These results, together with related progress in reinforcement learning and LLM-guided discovery of quantum error-correcting codes and encoding circuits [21, 22, 23], create an opportunity for end-to-end co-design of fault-tolerant computation. Choices that are usually made separately—the algorithm and its logical circuit, the error-correcting code and its method for universal logic, the supply of magic states, and the physical execution architecture—strongly determine one another’s costs. A programmatic evaluator that propagates logical errors, resource demand, and hardware requirements across these layers could allow an LLM search to redesign them together, potentially discovering fault-tolerant algorithms and architectures that cannot be found by optimizing each layer in isolation.

Methods

A classical function cannot generally be applied directly within a quantum algorithm, because quantum evolution must be reversible. Instead, a function ff is embedded in a reversible map |x⟩​|y⟩⟼|x⟩​|y⊕f⁡(x)⟩\ket{x}\ket{y}\longmapsto\ket{x}\ket{y\oplus f(x)}. A natural model for these subroutines is the kickmix circuit model of Babbush et al. [8], which augments reversible classical computation with measurement-based uncomputation (MBU) and diagonal sign gates. Despite these additional operations, kickmix circuits remain efficiently classically simulable. This allows candidate circuits to be tested for their action on coherent quantum superpositions, providing the reliable correctness signal needed for evolutionary search.

Circuits that implement the same specification can have very different time and space requirements. We use Toffoli count and peak qubit count as proxies for these costs. Toffoli gates require expensive non-Clifford resources, so their count tracks a large part of the logical work and often the runtime [24, 25]. The peak qubit count measures the data and ancillas that must coexist during execution and therefore approximates the required logical processor footprint [26]. The two resources also typically trade against each other: additional ancillas can avoid recomputation, while recycling ancillas can reduce space at the cost of additional gates. We multiply these quantities to obtain the T​QTQ-cost, which provides a single objective for comparing such designs.

Together, the correctness tests and T​QTQ-cost define a constrained optimization problem over circuit-generating programs. Motivated by recent advances in coding and reasoning agents and LLM-guided algorithmic discovery, we use an LLM to propose coordinated, task-specific redesigns within an evolutionary search [27, 28, 20].

Circuit model and validity

A compilation task specifies a reversible action on computational-basis states: a permutation π\pi and, when needed, a Boolean phase gg. A circuit may use aa ancilla qubits, but must return them to zero:

V​|x⟩​|0a⟩=(−1)g⁡(x)​|π⁡(x)⟩​|0a⟩.V\ket{x}\ket{0^{a}}=(-1)^{g(x)}\ket{\pi(x)}\ket{0^{a}}. (10)

Every ancilla must return to |0⟩\ket{0} because quantum operations must be unitary, and thus reversible. For a numerical approximation, the required output relation may instead specify an error bound; interface preservation, phase correctness, and ancilla uncomputation remain exact. We separately allow some circuits to fail on a bounded fraction of inputs drawn from a stated distribution; this fraction is the failure budget. Following Babbush et al. [8], the kickmix model permits three classes of operation:

  1. 1.

    classical reversible gates: XX, CNOT, Toffoli, and swap;

  2. 2.

    diagonal sign gates: ZZ, CZ, CCZ, and global sign flips; and

  3. 3.

    destructive XX-basis measurements.

Before any measurement, the evolution of a computational-basis input is simple. Reversible gates update its stored bit string, while diagonal gates update only its sign, so the state remains of the form (−1)ϕ​|x⟩(-1)^{\phi}\ket{x}. A classical simulator therefore need only track the current bits xx and the sign ϕ\phi, rather than a full state vector. The operations apply phase kickback while mixing basis states, giving kickmix its name.

To illustrate why uncomputation is costly, consider a temporary AND. A Toffoli computes t=u​vt=uv into an ancilla. After tt has been used, applying the same Toffoli again returns that qubit to zero:

|u,v⟩​|0⟩→𝐓𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐢|u,v⟩​|u​v⟩→use ​u​v|u,v⟩​|u​v⟩→𝐓𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐢|u,v⟩​|0⟩.\ket{u,v}\ket{0}\xrightarrow{\mathbf{Toffoli}}\ket{u,v}\ket{uv}\xrightarrow{\text{use }uv}\ket{u,v}\ket{uv}\xrightarrow{\mathbf{Toffoli}}\ket{u,v}\ket{0}. (11)

Computing and uncomputing this temporary AND therefore costs two Toffolis.

MBU, introduced by Gidney [29], replaces the second Toffoli with a destructive XX-basis measurement and a cheap phase correction. Measuring tt produces a uniformly random outcome rr and releases the ancilla, which can be restored to |0⟩\ket{0}:

|u,v⟩​|0⟩→𝐓𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐢|u,v⟩​|u​v⟩→use ​u​v|u,v⟩​|u​v⟩→X​-measure ​r(−1)r​u​v​|u,v⟩​|0⟩→CZ​if ​r=1|u,v⟩​|0⟩.\ket{u,v}\ket{0}\xrightarrow{\mathbf{Toffoli}}\ket{u,v}\ket{uv}\xrightarrow{\text{use }uv}\ket{u,v}\ket{uv}\xrightarrow{\ X\text{-measure }r\ }(-1)^{ruv}\ket{u,v}\ket{0}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{CZ}\ \text{if }r=1}\ket{u,v}\ket{0}. (12)

Because CZ is Clifford, the temporary AND is computed and cleared using only one Toffoli. By linearity, the same reasoning applies component by component when the retained bits are in superposition.

More generally, suppose an ancilla contains a Boolean function f⁡(y)f(y) of retained basis data yy. If mm records any earlier measurement outcomes, the simulator represents the ancilla’s destructive XX-basis measurement by the transition

((y,f⁡(y)),m,ϕ)⟼(y,m​r,ϕ⊕r​f​(y)),Pr⁡(r=0)=Pr⁡(r=1)=12.((y,f(y)),m,\phi)\longmapsto(y,mr,\phi\oplus rf(y)),\qquad\Pr(r=0)=\Pr(r=1)=\frac{1}{2}. (13)

On a coherent input, the retained state is therefore

∑yαy​(−1)r​f​(y)​|y⟩.\sum_{y}\alpha_{y}(-1)^{rf(y)}\ket{y}. (14)

When r=1r=1, a classically conditioned diagonal circuit for (−1)f⁡(y)(-1)^{f(y)} cancels this sign.

For a fixed computational-basis input and a particular sequence of measurement outcomes mm, we call the resulting evolution a computational-basis trajectory. A kickmix circuit may perform several such measurements. Their outcomes may be combined by classical XOR and may control diagonal corrections, but cannot control gates that change the stored basis string. Every measurement record therefore induces the same basis permutation:

Vm​|x⟩=(−1)ϕ⁡(x,m)​|π⁡(x)⟩.V_{m}\ket{x}=(-1)^{\phi(x,m)}\ket{\pi(x)}. (15)

Exact coherent correctness additionally requires

ϕ⁡(x,m)=g⁡(x)\phi(x,m)=g(x) (16)

for every allowed input and every record of nonzero probability. The measurement register then factors from the logical output. Allowing an outcome to control a basis-changing gate would instead make the permutation depend on the record and could leave the logical output correlated with the measurement environment.

Validation and statistical guarantees

The circuits are ultimately applied to coherent superpositions, whereas the evaluator follows one computational-basis trajectory at a time. Each test must therefore capture enough information to determine the trajectory’s coherent action. For a basis input xx and measurement record mm, the evaluator checks that the output matches the target, required inputs are unchanged, every ancilla has returned to |0⟩\ket{0}, and the phase agrees with the target exactly. These checks compare the complete final state rather than only its classical output. An ancilla that retains input-dependent information can become entangled with the logical registers, while an incorrect sign can alter subsequent interference without changing any output bit. Resetting or tracing out a dirty ancilla is therefore not a substitute for uncomputing it.

If every pair (x,m)(x,m) passes these tests, the measurement record factors from the logical output, and linearity extends agreement on every trajectory to any coherent input. For large input domains, however, the evaluator samples these trajectories rather than checking them all.

Consider a coherent input |ψ⟩=∑xαx​|x⟩\ket{\psi}=\sum_{x}\alpha_{x}\ket{x}, with 𝒟⁡(x)=|αx|2\mathcal{D}(x)=|\alpha_{x}|^{2}, and let ℳ\mathcal{M} be the set of possible measurement records. After deferring the measurements, the candidate and target states can be written as

|ΦV⟩=1|ℳ|​∑x,mαx​Vm​|x⟩​|m⟩,|ΦU⟩=1|ℳ|​∑x,mαx​U​|x⟩​|m⟩.\ket{\Phi_{V}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{M}|}}\sum_{x,m}\alpha_{x}V_{m}\ket{x}\ket{m},\qquad\ket{\Phi_{U}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{M}|}}\sum_{x,m}\alpha_{x}U\ket{x}\ket{m}. (17)

Let BB be the set of pairs (x,m)(x,m) on which Vm​|x⟩≠U​|x⟩V_{m}\ket{x}\neq U\ket{x}, and let

ε=1|ℳ|​∑(x,m)∈B|αx|2\varepsilon=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|}\sum_{(x,m)\in B}|\alpha_{x}|^{2} (18)

be the probability of BB under 𝒟\mathcal{D} and the uniform distribution over measurement records. Projecting onto the span of these defective trajectories gives

‖|ΦV⟩−|ΦU⟩‖≤2​ε.\bigl\|\ket{\Phi_{V}}-\ket{\Phi_{U}}\bigr\|\leq 2\sqrt{\varepsilon}. (19)

Consequently, the state fidelity is at least (1−2​ε)2(1-2\varepsilon)^{2}. Any subsequent measurement distribution changes by at most 2​ε2\sqrt{\varepsilon} in total variation distance. We bound ε\varepsilon by drawing xx from 𝒟\mathcal{D} and sampling every measurement outcome uniformly, exactly as in a basis trajectory. For a candidate fixed before the test draw, kk independent tests all pass with probability (1−ε)k(1-\varepsilon)^{k}. Thus, if all kk tests pass, then with confidence 1−δ1-\delta

ε≤1−δ1/k≈ln⁡(1/δ)k.\varepsilon\leq 1-\delta^{1/k}\approx\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{k}. (20)

More generally, if a test with kk random samples accepts at most bb failures, a candidate with true failure probability ε\varepsilon passes with probability

Pk,b​(ε)=∑j=0b(kj)​εj​(1−ε)k−j.P_{k,b}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{j=0}^{b}\binom{k}{j}\varepsilon^{j}(1-\varepsilon)^{k-j}. (21)

Cost model and scoring

We define the T​QTQ-cost of a circuit by

T​Q=Toffoli count×peak qubit count,TQ=\text{Toffoli count}\times\text{peak qubit count}, (22)

where TT counts Toffoli and CCZ gates equally and QQ is the largest number of logical qubits allocated at once.

We weight space and time equally in this cost function for simplicity. In practice, their relative importance depends on the hardware and application. When qubits are scarce, for example, a cost of the form (qubit count)κ×Toffoli count(\text{qubit count})^{\kappa}\times\text{Toffoli count} with κ>1\kappa>1 may be more appropriate; resource estimates for factoring have used κ\kappa between 1 and 3 [30, 6]. Either TT or QQ can also be replaced with other measures of time or space. In particular, when there is limited magic-state-factory throughput (as is typically the case), runtime is bottlenecked by the Toffoli count, motivating its widespread use as a time proxy [24, 25]. However, with enough factories to supply magic states in parallel, Toffoli depth rather than Toffoli count limits runtime. Similarly, for architectures with cheap cold storage for inactive qubits [31], QQ can be replaced by active volume [32], which counts only the qubits participating in logical operations.

The search is not tied to the specific form of the T​QTQ-cost: it can run with any computable objective. A later case study illustrates the available trade-offs: the modular-inversion search (SI II) produces a family of circuits along a Toffoli–qubit frontier (SI II.1), and an objective that weights qubit count more heavily selects a lower-qubit member of that family.

Evolutionary search

We encode each candidate as Python code that constructs a circuit. Functions, loops, and named registers preserve the organization of the computation, allowing the LLM to reason about arithmetic subroutines and their composition without reconstructing that structure from a flattened gate sequence. For example, changing a shared arithmetic routine changes every place where it is used, while reorganizing calls to that routine can change when intermediate values are computed, retained, and uncomputed. The representation thus makes coordinated changes expressible as revisions to the underlying algorithm.

We search over these circuit-generating programs with OpenEvolve [33], using Claude Mythos 5 [28] to propose architectures and program rewrites. Each of the eight searches uses a fixed, hand-written task specification, and all share the same generic circuit-building interface. During ideation, the LLM receives only the specification, circuit model, and correctness criteria, and proposes several distinct circuit architectures. The LLM has no access to the evaluator beyond the feedback returned after each submission. Starting from a blank program, it chooses the algorithm, representation, and circuit structure and produces the discovered circuits without substantive human intervention.

Each architecture proposed during ideation founds a separate family of candidate programs. Later iterations improve descendants of the first working implementation. Keeping the families separate at first gives each approach time to mature, even if its earliest circuits are less efficient than those based on another approach. Periodically, leading programs are shared across families, allowing successful ideas from different approaches to combine.

The search retains candidate programs and their evaluation results, tracking which family each belongs to and which earlier program it was derived from. It also saves feedback on failures and short notes in which the LLM records useful insights. These programs, results, and notes carry information between iterations; the sessions do not share a continuously growing conversation.

Each iteration starts a new LLM agent session with the task specification, a parent program to improve, and its evaluation feedback. The agent also receives alternative programs from the archive and their resource costs, brief summaries of earlier attempts, and recorded insights where available. This context is limited; the agent never sees the complete search history. Within the session, it may rewrite the program, run drafts on test inputs, query a classical oracle for the required function on chosen inputs, and use the results to revise its design. It may also delegate focused subtasks to subagents. The iteration ends with submission of a revised program. The evaluator rejects a circuit that does not meet the task specification; a valid one is scored by its T​QTQ-cost and considered for retention in its family. Thus the LLM is free to propose broad changes without having to judge their correctness: the evaluator supplies an independent test of every completed design. shows the ideation and rewrite calls and a concrete feedback-and-repair cycle for a small finite-field inversion task.

To decide which valid candidates remain available within each family, the search retains circuits with different trade-offs between Toffoli count and qubit count. We implement this selection with MAP-Elites [34], which divides the (T,Q)(T,Q) resource plane into cells and keeps the circuit with the lowest T​QTQ-cost in each cell. A space-efficient circuit can therefore remain available for later development even when its higher Toffoli count gives it a worse T​QTQ-cost.

Because the families preserve alternatives, progress need not be monotonic in either resource. The Gaussian lineage in , for example, contains descendants that temporarily worsen Toffoli count or qubit count before reaching a region of lower T​QTQ-cost. We report the lowest T​QTQ-cost reached across all families at the end of the search.

Supplementary Information

I Syndrome decoding for DQI

Consider an optimization problem over a finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. An assignment x∈𝔽qnx\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} produces mm linear values B​xBx. Given a set Fi⊂𝔽qF_{i}\subset\mathbb{F}_{q} of acceptable values for each constraint, let f⁡(x)=|{i:(B​x)i∈Fi}|f(x)=|\{i:(Bx)_{i}\in F_{i}\}| count the constraints satisfied by xx; the goal is to maximize f⁡(x)f(x). This family, known as max-LINSAT, includes linear constraint-satisfaction problems such as Max-Cut and max-XORSAT, as well as nearest-codeword problems and polynomial fitting over finite fields. Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is a quantum algorithm that aims to solve these optimization problems by arranging for constructive interference on assignments satisfying many constraints and destructive interference on assignments satisfying fewer [1].

DQI prepares a superposition over sparse vectors e∈𝔽qme\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m}, each supported on at most ℓ\ell constraints. Here H=B𝖳H=B^{\mathsf{T}} can be viewed as a parity-check matrix, making ee a low-weight error and H​eHe its syndrome. If the associated code has minimum distance dmin≥2​ℓ+1d_{\min}\geq 2\ell+1, a decoder can recover ee uniquely from that syndrome. DQI uses the decoder in the following state-preparation sequence:

∑wt⁡(e)≤ℓae​|e⟩​|0⟩\displaystyle\sum_{\operatorname{wt}(e)\leq\ell}a_{e}\ket{e}\ket{0} →s=H​e∑wt⁡(e)≤ℓae​|e⟩​|H​e⟩\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\ s=He\ }\sum_{\operatorname{wt}(e)\leq\ell}a_{e}\ket{e}\ket{He} (23)
→uncompute ​e|0⟩​∑wt⁡(e)≤ℓae​|H​e⟩→QFT−1∑xAx​|x⟩.\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\text{uncompute }e}\ket{0}\sum_{\operatorname{wt}(e)\leq\ell}a_{e}\ket{He}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{QFT}^{-1}}\sum_{x}A_{x}\ket{x}.

The middle step must erase ee while retaining its syndrome s=H​es=He; otherwise the different contributions remain distinguishable and cannot interfere. The inverse quantum Fourier transform (QFT) then produces amplitudes AxA_{x} that favor assignments satisfying more constraints. The dominant cost in Equation 23 is uncomputing ee, which requires solving a classical decoding problem; DQI thus reduces optimization to decoding.

The space-efficient construction of Khattar et al. [13] replaces the middle decoding-and-uncomputation step with a phase correction. It generates one field symbol eie_{i} at a time, adds its contribution to ss, and then removes it with an XX-basis measurement. This avoids retaining all mm symbols of ee, but the measurement outcomes cic_{i} leave a known phase. We expand each symbol of e∈𝔽qme\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m} in the fixed binary basis used by the circuit, so that cc and ee are bit strings of equal length; the phase is then (−1)⟨c,e⟩2(-1)^{\langle c,e\rangle_{2}}, where ⟨⋅,⋅⟩2\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{2} denotes the binary inner product. We call cc the mask. In this section, we use a fixed, randomly chosen mask. A reversible decoder must remove this phase using ss, after which the inverse Fourier transform produces the desired interference over assignments xx. The case studies below isolate and optimize this decoder-dependent phase correction. We require

|s⟩⟼(−1)⟨c,e⁡(s)⟩2​|s⟩.\ket{s}\longmapsto(-1)^{\langle c,e(s)\rangle_{2}}\ket{s}. (24)

We study two instances of DQI. In optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), xx specifies a univariate polynomial and the constraints restrict its values at prescribed points on a line; the associated code is a Reed–Solomon code. Hermitian optimal polynomial intersection (HOPI) generalizes this picture from a line to a Hermitian curve: xx specifies a function on the curve, the constraints restrict its values at curve points, and the corresponding code is a Hermitian code [41]. Table S1 lists the parameters of the two benchmark instances.

We test implementations on syndromes drawn from the DQI input distribution (defined by |ae|2|a_{e}|^{2}) and accept implementations with at most 100 detected wrong signs in 100,000 tests. Let ε\varepsilon be the failure probability: the total probability, under this distribution, of the inputs on which the circuit fails. A failure applies the wrong sign or resets an ancilla that still holds input-dependent data. The discovered circuit satisfies [16]

|⟨f⟩impl−⟨f⟩|≤4​ε​⟨f⟩.\bigl|\langle f\rangle_{\mathrm{impl}}-\langle f\rangle\bigr|\leq 4\varepsilon\langle f\rangle. (25)

Under our testing framework, a wrong sign is detected with probability at least 12\tfrac{1}{2}: for any fixed input, whether the sign is wrong is given by a constant plus a linear function (modulo 2) of the uniformly random measurement record, and a reset of a nonzero qubit adds a fresh uniformly random bit to the sign. Thus the acceptance limit of 100 failures in 100,000 tests gives ε≤2.434×10−3\varepsilon\leq 2.434\times 10^{-3} at 97.5%97.5\% confidence. At that value, Equation 25 bounds the loss in satisfied fraction by 5.6×10−35.6\times 10^{-3} (Reed–Solomon) and 7.0×10−37.0\times 10^{-3} (Hermitian)—at most 7.4%7.4\% and 4.9%4.9\% of the two instances’ advantage over single-trial Prange.

I.1 Reed–Solomon decoding for OPI

We use the Reed–Solomon instance and reversible decoder of Khattar et al. [13] as our baseline. Let γ\gamma be a primitive element of 𝔽212\mathbb{F}_{2^{12}}. An error word e∈𝔽2124095e\in\mathbb{F}_{2^{12}}^{4095} produces 70 syndromes

Si=∑j=04094ejγi​j,i=1,…,70.S_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{4094}e_{j}\gamma^{ij},\qquad i=1,\ldots,70. (26)

This syndrome map defines a [4095,4025,71]212[4095,4025,71]_{2^{12}} Reed–Solomon code. The 70 twelve-bit syndromes occupy 840 qubits. Assuming the error weight is at most 35, the decoding task is to recover the error from the syndromes.

Decoding proceeds in two stages: first find the positions of the errors, then recover their values in 𝔽212\mathbb{F}_{2^{12}}. The first stage packages the unknown set of error positions into a single polynomial. For each nonzero error symbol eje_{j}, include one factor 1−γj​z1-\gamma^{j}z, giving

σ(z)=∏j:ej≠0(1−γjz).\sigma(z)=\prod_{j:e_{j}\neq 0}(1-\gamma^{j}z). (27)

The factor associated with position jj vanishes at z=γ−jz=\gamma^{-j}, so the roots of σ\sigma identify exactly the positions at which the error word is nonzero. The decoder’s first task is therefore to recover this locator polynomial from the syndromes. The input |s⟩\ket{s} supplies the first 70 syndromes, which we collect into a polynomial

S⁡(z)=S1+S2​z+⋯+S70​z69.S(z)=S_{1}+S_{2}z+\cdots+S_{70}z^{69}. (28)

Summing the geometric series in Equation 26 shows that the product σ⁡(z)​S​(z)\sigma(z)S(z) agrees, through degree 69, with a polynomial ω⁡(z)\omega(z) of degree less than deg⁡σ\deg\sigma, called the error-evaluator polynomial:

σ⁡(z)​S​(z)=ω⁡(z)(modz70).\sigma(z)S(z)=\omega(z)\pmod{z^{70}}. (29)

The decoder recovers the locator σ\sigma of least degree and the corresponding evaluator ω\omega from this key equation. The baseline does so with the extended Euclidean algorithm (EEA) applied to S⁡(z)S(z) and z70z^{70}. It repeatedly divides the higher-degree polynomial by the lower-degree one, replaces the former by the remainder, and stops when the remainder has degree below 35. That remainder is ω\omega, and the coefficient that accompanies it is σ\sigma, up to normalization. The promise of at most 35 errors ensures deg⁡σ≤35\deg\sigma\leq 35 and determines this pair uniquely.

The baseline next locates the errors by evaluating σ\sigma at every possible position. Associate position jj with the field point βj=γ−j\beta_{j}=\gamma^{-j} (since γ\gamma is primitive, these points enumerate all 4,095 nonzero field elements). The scan visits them one by one and tests whether σ⁡(βj)=0\sigma(\beta_{j})=0. It need not evaluate σ\sigma independently each time: advancing to βj+1=γ−1​βj\beta_{j+1}=\gamma^{-1}\beta_{j} multiplies its degree-rr term by the fixed constant γ−r\gamma^{-r}. This efficient scan is known as a Chien search [43]. Finding a root reveals an error’s position but not its value. At βj\beta_{j}, the evaluator ω⁡(βj)\omega(\beta_{j}) contains the error value multiplied by the contributions of the other locator factors, while the formal derivative σ′​(βj)\sigma^{\prime}(\beta_{j})—the usual coefficientwise polynomial derivative over the field—contains those same factors without the error value. Their ratio therefore isolates eje_{j}, up to a fixed factor κj\kappa_{j} that depends only on the position:

ej=κj​ω⁡(βj)σ′​(βj).e_{j}=\kappa_{j}\frac{\omega(\beta_{j})}{\sigma^{\prime}(\beta_{j})}. (30)

This recovery step is Forney’s formula [44]. The circuit immediately uses that value and the matching twelve-bit block cjc_{j} to apply the phase (24). It then reverses the computation to restore the syndrome and clear its ancillas.

The EEA is the dominant cost of this baseline because its classical control flow depends on the syndromes: different inputs require different shifts, swaps, and numbers of iterations. A quantum circuit must instead apply one fixed sequence of gates across the syndrome superposition. The baseline therefore spreads the Euclidean solve over 222 synchronized cycles, controlling each operation so that it acts only when needed. Our implementation of this baseline, based on the authors’ released code [35], uses 5.1 million Toffoli gates and 1,938 qubits at peak, with the forward Euclidean solve and its reversal accounting for 3.8 million of the Toffolis 11 1 This agrees with the decoder-stage estimate recomputed from the authors’ released code [35] (5.0 million Toffolis, 1,885 qubits) within about 2%2\% in Toffoli count; the qubit counts differ because the estimate takes stage-wise maxima while the composed circuit retains the Euclidean state during the scan..

The discovered circuit changes both stages of this baseline. First, it replaces the Euclidean solve with the arithmetically cheaper Berlekamp–Massey (BM) recurrence and arranges the recurrence so that reversibility does not require retaining much history state. Second, although the decoded error word contains 49,140 bits, DQI extracts only the single bit ⟨c,e⟩2\langle c,e\rangle_{2} from it. The circuit therefore computes this phase bit directly from the locator and syndromes rather than materializing the full decoded error, and it precomputes one reciprocal polynomial so that no field division is performed during the scan.

An alternative to solving the key equation by EEA is the standard BM algorithm, which recovers the locator from a linear recurrence among the syndromes. We first review how BM reads Equation 29 one coefficient at a time. Write σ⁡(z)=∑k=0Lσk​zk\sigma(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{L}\sigma_{k}z^{k}, where L=deg⁡σL=\deg\sigma. The coefficient of zr−1z^{r-1} in σ⁡(z)​S​(z)\sigma(z)S(z) is the convolution ∑k=0Lσk​Sr−k\sum_{k=0}^{L}\sigma_{k}S_{r-k}. Because deg⁡ω<L\deg\omega<L, the key equation requires every such coefficient from degree LL through degree 69 to vanish:

0=[zr−1]σ(z)S(z)=∑k=0LσkSr−k,r=L+1,…,70.0=[z^{r-1}]\,\sigma(z)S(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{L}\sigma_{k}S_{r-k},\qquad r=L+1,\ldots,70. (31)

Since we can set σ0=1\sigma_{0}=1 without loss of generality, and subtraction is the same as addition in 𝔽212\mathbb{F}_{2^{12}}, every syndrome after the first LL satisfies

Sr=σ1​Sr−1+⋯+σL​Sr−L.S_{r}=\sigma_{1}S_{r-1}+\cdots+\sigma_{L}S_{r-L}. (32)

Thus the locator coefficients give a rule for predicting each syndrome from the preceding LL syndromes. We call LL the order of this recurrence. BM finds this recurrence by maintaining a candidate locator σ\sigma and refining it as the syndromes are incorporated [46]. At the start of round rr, the candidate defines a lowest-order recurrence for the already processed syndromes S1,…,Sr−1S_{1},\ldots,S_{r-1}. The round tests whether that recurrence also fits SrS_{r}. The discrepancy Δ=∑k=0Lσk​Sr−k\Delta=\sum_{k=0}^{L}\sigma_{k}S_{r-k} is the sum in Equation 31 for round rr, computed with the current candidate. It measures the amount by which the recurrence fails: Δ=0\Delta=0 means that the current candidate already fits SrS_{r}, while Δ≠0\Delta\neq 0 requires the candidate to be refined.

When Δ≠0\Delta\neq 0, BM needs a correction that fixes the equation for SrS_{r} without invalidating any of the earlier equations. For this purpose, it retains an earlier candidate τ\tau as a correction template, together with the nonzero discrepancy δ\delta that candidate produced. At the start of each subsequent round, BM multiplies τ\tau by zz, shifting every coefficient one degree higher as the recurrence advances to the next syndrome. Thus, if the template was saved kk rounds earlier, it has acquired a factor zkz^{k} and is aligned with the current syndrome equation while leaving the earlier equations unchanged. BM then scales this aligned template by α=Δ/δ\alpha=\Delta/\delta and applies σ←σ−α​τ\sigma\leftarrow\sigma-\alpha\tau: at SrS_{r}, the correction contributes exactly α​δ=Δ\alpha\delta=\Delta and so cancels the discrepancy.

On a round with a nonzero discrepancy, BM must also decide whether the current candidate takes over as the template. A candidate of order LL that fits nn syndromes has predicted n−Ln-L of them. BM seeks the recurrence of lowest order, and a correction raises the order less when its template had predicted more syndromes at the time it was saved. BM therefore replaces the template when the current candidate has predicted more syndromes than the stored template had when it was saved, and retains it when the current candidate has predicted fewer. When the two counts are equal, either choice gives a correct decoder [46, p. 125]. Textbook BM retains in that case. The circuit instead chooses to replace, which reduces the history it must store (see “Reconstructing BM history” below).

The circuit makes this decision with a signed counter dd. The counter is nonnegative whenever a replacement is required and negative whenever the template must be retained; when the counts are equal it may have either sign. Starting from (σ,τ,δ,d)=(1,1,1,0)(\sigma,\tau,\delta,d)=(1,1,1,0), each round r=1,…,70r=1,\ldots,70 applies

τ~=zτ,Δ=∑i=0min⁡(deg⁡σ,r−1)σiSr−i,(σ,τ,δ,d)←{(σ,τ~,δ,d+1),Δ=0,(σ−(Δ/δ)​τ~,σ,Δ,−d),Δ≠0,d≥0,(σ−(Δ/δ)​τ~,τ~,δ,d+1),Δ≠0,d<0.\begin{gathered}\widetilde{\tau}=z\tau,\qquad\Delta=\sum_{i=0}^{\min(\deg\sigma,r-1)}\sigma_{i}S_{r-i},\\[2.84526pt] (\sigma,\tau,\delta,d)\leftarrow\begin{cases}(\sigma,\widetilde{\tau},\delta,d+1),&\Delta=0,\\ (\sigma-(\Delta/\delta)\widetilde{\tau},\sigma,\Delta,-d),&\Delta\neq 0,\ d\geq 0,\\ (\sigma-(\Delta/\delta)\widetilde{\tau},\widetilde{\tau},\delta,d+1),&\Delta\neq 0,\ d<0.\end{cases}\end{gathered} (33)

After the final round, σ\sigma is the error locator.

Adaptive coefficient ranges.

A naïve implementation would apply every BM update across all 36 possible coefficient positions in every round. Even in the worst case, this is unnecessary: after rr syndromes have been processed, only coefficients through degree min⁡(r,35)\min(r,35) can be active, so the update range need only grow by one position per round. The dashed line in Figure S1(b) shows this worst-case bound. On the DQI input distribution, however, the candidate polynomials typically grow more slowly still. A degree-LL locator σ\sigma has LL unknown coefficients after fixing σ0=1\sigma_{0}=1, while its evaluator ω\omega, whose degree is less than LL, has at most LL unknown coefficients. Since each syndrome supplies one coefficient constraint, rr syndromes typically determine a locator of degree L≈r/2L\approx r/2, consistent with the samples in Figure S1(b).

The discovered circuit exploits this typical behavior, at the price of failing on rare inputs. Before compiling the circuit, we classically simulate BM on the DQI input distribution to choose a cutoff kk for each round. The circuit then updates only the prefix σ0,…,σk\sigma_{0},\ldots,\sigma_{k}, treating higher coefficients as zero. The prefixes expand as the rounds progress, which produces the rising per-round cost in Figure S1(a).

Shared BM updates.

Compiled directly, the two correction cases of Equation 33 would produce two separately controlled arithmetic paths. Only one path acts on any basis state, but both would appear in the fixed circuit and contribute to its Toffoli count. The main text shows how the circuit avoids this (Equation 5). Under a flag that marks the replace case, it exchanges σ\sigma with the shifted template τ~\widetilde{\tau}. One shared update then subtracts a multiple of the template register from the locator register. The multiplier is α\alpha in the retain case and α−1\alpha^{-1} in the replace case. The replace result differs from the standard update only by the nonzero factor −α−1-\alpha^{-1} and therefore has the same roots.

The circuit also stores no discrepancy δ\delta. The rescaled update maintains the invariant

σ0​δ=1.\sigma_{0}\delta=1. (34)

The invariant holds initially. The shifted template has zero constant coefficient, so the retain case changes neither σ0\sigma_{0} nor δ\delta. In the replace case, the new constant coefficient comes entirely from the correction term: σ0←α−1​σ0=(δ/Δ)​σ0=Δ−1\sigma_{0}\leftarrow\alpha^{-1}\sigma_{0}=(\delta/\Delta)\sigma_{0}=\Delta^{-1}, while δ←Δ\delta\leftarrow\Delta. The circuit therefore reads δ=σ0−1\delta=\sigma_{0}^{-1} from the locator. In each round it forms the product Δ​σ0\Delta\sigma_{0}, which equals α\alpha, and inverts it. A controlled selection between the product and its inverse supplies the multiplier for the shared update.

Reconstructing BM history.

Reversing a round requires the discrepancy that the round used, which the round computes into a temporary register. Keeping a twelve-bit history word for every round would raise the qubit count to 2,677. A replace round leaves σ0=Δ−1\sigma_{0}=\Delta^{-1} by Equation 34, so the locator determines the round’s discrepancy. The circuit therefore erases the temporary discrepancy register by MBU, and the reverse pass recomputes the erased value from the locator. A round with Δ=0\Delta=0 changes nothing and has nothing to recover.

A retain round with Δ≠0\Delta\neq 0 is the exception. No exchange occurs and σ0\sigma_{0} is unchanged, so the constant coefficient that reveals the discrepancy on a replace round carries no trace of it here. The current Δ\Delta remains only in the temporary discrepancy register, and the circuit stores it on the history stack before erasing that register. A stack that never overflows needs 35 entries, or 665 qubits.

Retain rounds are rare on the DQI input distribution. Starting from d=0d=0, a run of nonzero discrepancies repeatedly selects replace and leaves d=0d=0. A zero discrepancy raises dd; a later replacement can then make it negative, producing retain rounds while dd returns to zero. Such accidental zero discrepancies are uncommon over 𝔽212\mathbb{F}_{2^{12}} before the locator reaches its final degree. Once it has, subsequent discrepancies stay zero and do not start new runs of retain rounds. Consequently, most inputs need few saved discrepancies. The discovered circuit allocates only one stack entry, which costs 19 qubits (Figure S1(b)).

Across 400 million samples from the DQI input distribution, the two failure modes (overflow of the one-entry stack and activation of a coefficient beyond the cutoff) occur with a combined probability of 1.4×10−41.4\times 10^{-4}. This completes locator construction; the circuit next forms the evaluator ω\omega, which will be used together with σ\sigma to compute the required phase.

In-place construction of the evaluator polynomial.

The key equation (29) gives ω\omega by multiplying the locator by the syndrome polynomial. The circuit first normalizes σ\sigma so that σ0=1\sigma_{0}=1. This leaves the locator roots unchanged, and the corresponding ω\omega acquires the same nonzero factor, so the ratio ω/σ′\omega/\sigma^{\prime} used to recover the error values is unchanged. Write ω<35=(ω0,…,ω34)\omega_{<35}=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{34}) for the first 35 coefficients of ω\omega:

(σ,S1,…,S35,S36,…,S70)⟼(σ,ω<35=σ​Smodz35,S36,…,S70).(\sigma;S_{1},\ldots,S_{35};S_{36},\ldots,S_{70})\longmapsto(\sigma;\omega_{<35}=\sigma S\bmod z^{35};S_{36},\ldots,S_{70}). (35)

With this normalization, each output coefficient is

ωi=Si+1+∑j=1iσj​Si−j+1,0≤i<35,\omega_{i}=S_{i+1}+\sum_{j=1}^{i}\sigma_{j}S_{i-j+1},\qquad 0\leq i<35, (36)

so it equals the syndrome symbol being overwritten plus a function of earlier symbols. The transformation is therefore reversible: the circuit can overwrite the first 35 syndrome symbols with the first 35 coefficients of ω\omega and later restore them. This avoids a separate 420-qubit register for ω\omega. The same map extends to all 70 syndrome symbols; by the key equation, the coefficients of σ​S\sigma S from degree 35 through 69 vanish whenever the locator is correct, so the last 35 become zero and serve as workspace until the map is reversed.

Phase-only error recovery.

At this point the decoder could use σ\sigma and ω\omega to recover every error value. An ordinary decoder does so by applying Forney’s formula (30) to construct the twelve-bit field element eje_{j} at each located error. The DQI task (24), however, needs only the single accumulated parity ∑j⟨cj,ej⟩2\sum_{j}\langle c_{j},e_{j}\rangle_{2}. Constructing all twelve bits of each eje_{j} only to retain one parity would waste most of this work, so the discovered circuit computes the required phase bit directly.

Any parity of a field element can be expressed as a field trace after multiplication by a fixed constant. In particular, with Tr⁡(x)=∑r=011x2r∈𝔽2\operatorname{Tr}(x)=\sum_{r=0}^{11}x^{2^{r}}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}, the twelve mask bits cjc_{j} determine a unique element μj∈𝔽212\mu_{j}\in\mathbb{F}_{2^{12}} such that

⟨cj,ej⟩2=Tr⁡(μj​ej).\langle c_{j},e_{j}\rangle_{2}=\operatorname{Tr}(\mu_{j}e_{j}). (37)

Part of the total phase is linear in the supplied syndromes and can be applied with Clifford ZZ gates. Choosing that linear part offline cancels the mask at 71 positions and leaves residual constants μ~j\widetilde{\mu}_{j} at the remaining 4,024 positions to scan.

At each remaining position the circuit tests whether βj\beta_{j} is a root of the locator. If it is, the error word is nonzero there. Absorb the fixed factor κj\kappa_{j} from Forney’s formula into νj=μ~j​κj\nu_{j}=\widetilde{\mu}_{j}\kappa_{j}. Substituting that formula directly into the trace gives the residual phase bit

Tr⁡(μ~j​ej)=Tr⁡(νj​ω⁡(βj)σ′​(βj)),\operatorname{Tr}(\widetilde{\mu}_{j}e_{j})=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\nu_{j}\frac{\omega(\beta_{j})}{\sigma^{\prime}(\beta_{j})}\right), (38)

without materializing eje_{j}.

Precomputed reciprocal.

The quotient in Equation 38 is required only at the roots of σ\sigma, of which there are at most 35. A quantum circuit, however, applies one fixed gate sequence to every syndrome in the superposition, so it cannot skip the positions that are not roots. A direct implementation would therefore perform the division at each of the 4,024 positions, and this division would dominate the decoder’s cost.

The circuit instead performs one division before the scan. Because only the values at the roots matter, any function that agrees with 1/σ′1/\sigma^{\prime} there serves equally well. The roots of σ\sigma are distinct, so σ′\sigma^{\prime} is nonzero at each of them, and a single polynomial Ψ\Psi of degree less than deg⁡σ\deg\sigma takes the value 1/σ′​(β)1/\sigma^{\prime}(\beta) at every root β\beta. Equivalently, Ψ​σ′≡1(modσ)\Psi\sigma^{\prime}\equiv 1\pmod{\sigma}. Evaluating Ψ\Psi and ω\omega at a fixed point is linear in their coefficients and uses only CNOTs, so the residual phase bit becomes

Tr⁡(μ~j​ej)=Tr⁡(νj​ω​(βj)​Ψ​(βj)),\operatorname{Tr}(\widetilde{\mu}_{j}e_{j})=\operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl(\nu_{j}\,\omega(\beta_{j})\,\Psi(\beta_{j})\bigr), (39)

which is bilinear in ω⁡(βj)\omega(\beta_{j}) and Ψ⁡(βj)\Psi(\beta_{j}). In a basis of 𝔽212\mathbb{F}_{2^{12}} over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}, it splits into 12 terms, each the product of one parity of the bits of ω⁡(βj)\omega(\beta_{j}) with one parity of the bits of Ψ⁡(βj)\Psi(\beta_{j}). The parities cost only CNOTs, and each product costs one Toffoli, applied only when the root test succeeds. The root test itself is a zero test on the twelve bits of σ⁡(βj)\sigma(\beta_{j}) and costs 11 Toffolis, so each position costs 11+12=2311+12=23 Toffolis.

Computing Ψ\Psi is itself a division: Ψ\Psi is the inverse of σ′\sigma^{\prime} modulo σ\sigma. The circuit computes it with the EEA (the algorithm that BM replaced for the key equation) on a smaller problem. Two observations make it affordable.

The Toffoli cost of the EEA grows roughly with the square of the operand degree. The first observation halves that degree, which cuts the Toffoli cost to about a quarter. In characteristic 2, squaring is linear: (a+b)2=a2+b2(a+b)^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}. It therefore acts on the twelve bits of a field element as a fixed linear map, as does its inverse, the square root, and both cost only CNOTs. Group the coefficients of σ\sigma by the parity of their degree:

σ⁡(z)=(σ0+σ2​z2+σ4​z4+⋯)+z⁡(σ1+σ3​z2+σ5​z4+⋯).\sigma(z)=\bigl(\sigma_{0}+\sigma_{2}z^{2}+\sigma_{4}z^{4}+\cdots\bigr)+z\bigl(\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{3}z^{2}+\sigma_{5}z^{4}+\cdots\bigr). (40)

Each group is a polynomial in z2z^{2} and hence a square, σ0+σ2​z2+⋯=(σ0+σ2​z+⋯)2\sigma_{0}+\sigma_{2}z^{2}+\cdots=\bigl(\sqrt{\sigma_{0}}+\sqrt{\sigma_{2}}\,z+\cdots\bigr)^{2}, so σ⁡(z)=E​(z)2+z​O​(z)2\sigma(z)=E(z)^{2}+z\,O(z)^{2} with Ei=σ2​iE_{i}=\sqrt{\sigma_{2i}}, Oi=σ2​i+1O_{i}=\sqrt{\sigma_{2i+1}}, and deg⁡E,deg⁡O≤17\deg E,\deg O\leq 17. In characteristic 2 the derivative of any square is zero, since (f2)′=2​f​f′(f^{2})^{\prime}=2ff^{\prime}, so σ′=O2\sigma^{\prime}=O^{2}. The polynomials EE and OO share no factor, because a common factor would divide both σ\sigma and σ′\sigma^{\prime}. The EEA on this half-degree pair (E,O)(E,O) returns AA and BB of degree at most 17 with A​E+B​O=1AE+BO=1. Then B​O=1+A​EBO=1+AE, so (B2+z​A2)​σ′=(B​O)2+z​A2​O2=1+A2​E2+z​A2​O2=1+A2​σ(B^{2}+zA^{2})\,\sigma^{\prime}=(BO)^{2}+zA^{2}O^{2}=1+A^{2}E^{2}+zA^{2}O^{2}=1+A^{2}\sigma, and B2+z​A2B^{2}+zA^{2} agrees with Ψ\Psi at every root of σ\sigma. Forming EE and OO from σ\sigma, and B2+z​A2B^{2}+zA^{2} from (A,B)(A,B), uses only square roots and squares. The only costly step, the EEA, thus runs on degree-17 rather than degree-35 operands.

The second observation concerns qubit usage. A fresh register for Ψ\Psi would raise the peak qubit count by 420. Instead, the circuit makes room inside the syndrome register itself. As described above, the in-place product over all 70 syndrome symbols leaves ω\omega in the first 35 and zeros in the last 35 on every correct decode. The circuit stores AA and BB in these zeroed words and evaluates Ψ⁡(βj)=B​(βj)2+βj​A​(βj)2\Psi(\beta_{j})=B(\beta_{j})^{2}+\beta_{j}A(\beta_{j})^{2} at each position with CNOTs only. After the scan, it reverses the Euclidean pass, which returns these words to zero, and then reverses the product to restore the syndromes.

Unlike the baseline’s Euclidean solve, this pass follows a fixed schedule. Every input runs the same 17 elimination blocks. Each block parks its quotients in the coefficient words that it clears, so the pass needs no separate history.

In total, the 4,024-position scan costs 93,000 Toffolis, and the Euclidean pass 44,000 in each direction, compared with 1.3 million for the baseline’s scan. The scan’s Toffoli count barely depends on the choice of cc: every scanned position uses the same 23-Toffoli circuit, and a different cc changes the number of scanned positions by at most one.

The discovered circuit uses 440,000 Toffolis and 1,837 qubits, for a T​QTQ-cost of 8.1×1088.1\times 10^{8}. Relative to the Reed–Solomon baseline, this reduces the Toffoli count by 12×12\times, the qubit count by 5.2%5.2\%, and the T​QTQ-cost by 12×12\times. In 100,000 tests of the complete circuit, seven produce the wrong sign.

I.2 Hermitian-code decoding for HOPI

HOPI requires the same phase (24) as the Reed–Solomon instance above, but its error word belongs to a 512-symbol Hermitian code over 𝔽64\mathbb{F}_{64}. A Reed–Solomon code with 512 positions would require symbols of about nine bits, since each position needs a distinct field element. A Hermitian code instead obtains 512 positions while retaining six-bit symbols by using the points (x,y)∈𝔽642(x,y)\in\mathbb{F}_{64}^{2} on

y8=x9+y.y^{8}=x^{9}+y. (41)

Polynomials in xx and yy are ordered by a weighted degree, the analogue of polynomial degree for Reed–Solomon codes. Here xx has weight 8 and yy has weight 9, so the monomial xa​ybx^{a}y^{b} has weighted degree 8​a+9​b8a+9b. These weights give the leading terms y8y^{8} and x9x^{9} of Equation 41 the same weighted degree, 72. Each finite point Pj=(xj,yj)P_{j}=(x_{j},y_{j}) is one code position. The syndrome construction is the two-variable analogue of the Reed–Solomon map above. A function ψ⁡(x,y)\psi(x,y) assigns a field value to every position and therefore defines one parity check

S⁡(ψ)=∑j=1512ej​ψ​(Pj).S(\psi)=\sum_{j=1}^{512}e_{j}\psi(P_{j}). (42)

The value S⁡(ψ)S(\psi) is one syndrome symbol. This instance uses the 123 monomials ψa,b​(x,y)=xa​yb\psi_{a,b}(x,y)=x^{a}y^{b} of weighted degree 8​a+9​b≤1508a+9b\leq 150 [41]. We enumerate them as ψ0,…,ψ122\psi_{0},\ldots,\psi_{122} in increasing weighted degree 22 2 Here a≥0a\geq 0 and 0≤b≤70\leq b\leq 7.. The input |s⟩\ket{s} supplies the 123 symbols

Sk:=S(ψk),k=0,…,122.S_{k}:=S(\psi_{k}),\qquad k=0,\ldots,122. (43)

This syndrome map defines a [512,389,dmin≥96]64[512,389,d_{\min}\geq 96]_{64} Hermitian code, so the syndrome uniquely determines every error affecting at most 47 positions. The 123 six-bit syndromes occupy 738 qubits. Table S2 lists the correspondences with the Reed–Solomon decoder that the rest of this subsection uses.

As in Reed–Solomon decoding, the first task is to find a locator σ\sigma that vanishes at every error point; here it is a function of two variables on the curve. Multiplying each root condition by ej​ψk′​(Pj)e_{j}\psi_{k^{\prime}}(P_{j}) and summing over positions gives, for σ=∑kσk​ψk\sigma=\sum_{k}\sigma_{k}\psi_{k},

0=S⁡(σ​ψk′)=∑kσk​S​(ψk​ψk′).0=S(\sigma\psi_{k^{\prime}})=\sum_{k}\sigma_{k}S(\psi_{k}\psi_{k^{\prime}}). (44)

This has the same form as the Reed–Solomon recurrence (31): a sum of syndromes weighted by the locator coefficients. Whereas multiplying Reed–Solomon monomials simply shifts the syndrome index, the curve relation (41) reduces each product ψk​ψk′\psi_{k}\psi_{k^{\prime}} to one or two basis monomials. Beyond error weight 33, some of the syndromes that the recurrence needs have weighted degree above 150, which the input does not supply. The Feng–Rao baseline reconstructs these missing syndromes by majority voting among recurrence predictions, then uses the extended sequence to locate and evaluate the errors [39].

Our reversible implementation of this baseline uses 100 million Toffolis at a peak of 190,000 qubits, for a T​QTQ-cost of 2.0×10132.0\times 10^{13}. The large qubit count comes from retaining the intermediate states of the recurrence updates until the circuit reverses the computation.

The discovered circuit instead turns locator finding into a null-space problem for a symmetric matrix AA built directly from the supplied syndromes. It never stores AA; instead, it computes the effect of multiplying a vector by AA directly from the syndromes. Repeating this operation produces a sequence of vectors that must eventually become linearly dependent, and such a dependence yields the desired null vector. The circuit processes this sequence incrementally, retaining only a few vectors at a time and grouping several consecutive vectors when a vector cannot be processed alone. Once the null vector supplies a locator σ\sigma, the circuit still avoids constructing the whole evaluator ω\omega or the decoded error word. It scans the curve points in small batches called stripes, combines the locator and syndromes only for the current stripe, applies those points’ phase contributions, and clears the temporary data before continuing. The circuit thus has two stages: a locator walk that never stores the matrix, and a space-efficient phase scan. The walk freezes on the rare inputs that need extra work and repairs them at scheduled rounds. Its reversal recomputes most decisions and stores one bit per round.

The locator as a null vector.

The discovered circuit looks for the locator in a fixed space that is large enough to always contain one. Following the linear-algebra strategy of Skorobogatov and Vlăduţ [48], it uses the span of the 48 monomials ψ0,…,ψ47\psi_{0},\ldots,\psi_{47} of weighted degree at most 75. Writing σ=∑k=047σk​ψk\sigma=\sum_{k=0}^{47}\sigma_{k}\psi_{k}, each error point imposes one linear condition ∑k=047σk​ψk​(Pj)=0\sum_{k=0}^{47}\sigma_{k}\psi_{k}(P_{j})=0 on the 48 coefficients. There are at most 47 conditions on 48 unknowns, so a nonzero locator always exists.
