The error points are unknown, so the circuit cannot impose these conditions directly. It replaces them with a condition that it can compute from the syndromes. Define the symmetric 48×4848\times 48 matrix Ak​k′=S⁡(ψk​ψk′)A_{kk^{\prime}}=S(\psi_{k}\psi_{k^{\prime}}). Each product ψk​ψk′\psi_{k}\psi_{k^{\prime}} has weighted degree at most 150, so every entry of AA is a linear function of the supplied syndromes. The coefficient vector 𝝈=(σ0,…,σ47)𝖳\boldsymbol{\sigma}=(\sigma_{0},\ldots,\sigma_{47})^{\mathsf{T}} of every locator lies in the null space of AA, and almost always the converse holds as well.

To see this, let ℰ\mathcal{E} be the set of error points and let Mj​k=ψk​(Pj)M_{jk}=\psi_{k}(P_{j}) for Pj∈ℰP_{j}\in\mathcal{E}. Then

A=M𝖳diag(ej)M,M𝝈=(σ(Pj):Pj∈ℰ)𝖳.A=M^{\mathsf{T}}\operatorname{diag}(e_{j})\,M,\qquad M\boldsymbol{\sigma}=(\sigma(P_{j}):P_{j}\in\mathcal{E})^{\mathsf{T}}. (45)

A locator has M​𝝈=0M\boldsymbol{\sigma}=0 and therefore A​𝝈=0A\boldsymbol{\sigma}=0. Conversely, when the conditions σ⁡(Pj)=0\sigma(P_{j})=0 are independent, MM has full row rank. The error values are nonzero, so A​𝝈=0A\boldsymbol{\sigma}=0 then implies M​𝝈=0M\boldsymbol{\sigma}=0, and σ\sigma is a locator. The conditions are dependent with probability ≈8×10−8\approx 8\times 10^{-8} under the DQI input distribution.

Applying AA without storing it.

The circuit needs only the product A​𝒖A\boldsymbol{u} for a given vector 𝒖\boldsymbol{u}. Computing it directly would take 482=2,30448^{2}=2{,}304 field multiplications. Let U=∑kuk​ψkU=\sum_{k}u_{k}\psi_{k} be the function with coefficient vector 𝒖\boldsymbol{u}. Then (A​𝒖)k′=S⁡(ψk′​U)(A\boldsymbol{u})_{k^{\prime}}=S(\psi_{k^{\prime}}U): each entry is the syndrome of a product of two functions. Every such product lies in the span of the 123 monomials, so its values at 123 suitably chosen curve points R1,…,R123R_{1},\ldots,R_{123} determine it. On this span the syndrome is therefore a weighted sum of point values, S⁡(f)=∑i=1123ηi​f​(Ri)S(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{123}\eta_{i}f(R_{i}), with weights ηi\eta_{i} that are a fixed linear function of the supplied syndromes. Writing Φi​k=ψk​(Ri)\Phi_{ik}=\psi_{k}(R_{i}) gives

A​𝒖=Φ𝖳​diag⁡(𝜼)​Φ​𝒖.A\boldsymbol{u}=\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\eta})\Phi\boldsymbol{u}. (46)

Here Φ​𝒖\Phi\boldsymbol{u} evaluates UU at the points, the diagonal map multiplies each value by its weight, and Φ𝖳\Phi^{\mathsf{T}} returns the weighted values to the 48 coefficients. The maps Φ\Phi and Φ𝖳\Phi^{\mathsf{T}} are fixed and linear, so they cost only CNOTs. The only Toffolis are in the 123 pointwise products, each a 15-Toffoli multiplication in 𝔽64\mathbb{F}_{64} [49, 50]. One application of AA thus costs 123×15=1,845123\times 15=1{,}845 Toffolis. The same pattern recurs below, and we call it evaluation–interpolation: the circuit evaluates at fixed points, multiplies the values pointwise, and maps the products back linearly.

Lanczos recurrence.

A null vector of AA can be found from repeated applications of AA. Starting from a fixed seed 𝒚0\boldsymbol{y}_{0}, generate the Krylov vectors 𝒚0,A​𝒚0,A2​𝒚0,…\boldsymbol{y}_{0},A\boldsymbol{y}_{0},A^{2}\boldsymbol{y}_{0},\ldots. They all lie in a 48-dimensional space, so they must become linearly dependent: there are coefficients, not all zero, with λ0​𝒚0+λ1​A​𝒚0+⋯+λN​AN​𝒚0=0\lambda_{0}\boldsymbol{y}_{0}+\lambda_{1}A\boldsymbol{y}_{0}+\cdots+\lambda_{N}A^{N}\boldsymbol{y}_{0}=0. If the seed is not orthogonal to the entire null space, symmetry forces λ0=0\lambda_{0}=0. To see this, choose 𝒗\boldsymbol{v} in the null space of AA with 𝒗𝖳​𝒚0≠0\boldsymbol{v}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{y}_{0}\neq 0. Symmetry gives 𝒗𝖳​Ar​𝒚0=0\boldsymbol{v}^{\mathsf{T}}A^{r}\boldsymbol{y}_{0}=0 for r≥1r\geq 1, so the inner product of the dependence with 𝒗\boldsymbol{v} leaves λ0​𝒗𝖳​𝒚0=0\lambda_{0}\boldsymbol{v}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{y}_{0}=0. Then

𝝈=∑r=1Nλr​Ar−1​𝒚0,A​𝝈=∑r=1Nλr​Ar​𝒚0=0\boldsymbol{\sigma}=\sum_{r=1}^{N}\lambda_{r}A^{r-1}\boldsymbol{y}_{0},\qquad A\boldsymbol{\sigma}=\sum_{r=1}^{N}\lambda_{r}A^{r}\boldsymbol{y}_{0}=0 (47)

is the desired null vector. In the rare case where λ0≠0\lambda_{0}\neq 0, the decoding fails.

Used directly, this would require storing every Krylov vector until the dependence appears. The Lanczos algorithm avoids that. It maintains an orthogonal basis 𝒘0,𝒘1,…\boldsymbol{w}_{0},\boldsymbol{w}_{1},\ldots whose first r+1r+1 vectors span the first r+1r+1 Krylov vectors: it applies AA to the newest basis vector and subtracts the components along the existing basis. Because AA is symmetric, A​𝒘rA\boldsymbol{w}_{r} is already orthogonal to every basis vector except 𝒘r−1\boldsymbol{w}_{r-1} and 𝒘r\boldsymbol{w}_{r}, so

A​𝒘r∈span⁡{𝒘r−1,𝒘r,𝒘r+1}.A\boldsymbol{w}_{r}\in\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{w}_{r-1},\boldsymbol{w}_{r},\boldsymbol{w}_{r+1}\}. (48)

Constructing the next vector therefore needs only the current and the preceding basis vectors. A zero result means that the Krylov vectors have become dependent.

The null vector can be built in the same pass. By Equation 48, the coefficients ξr\xi_{r} of a null vector 𝝈=∑rξr​𝒘r\boldsymbol{\sigma}=\sum_{r}\xi_{r}\boldsymbol{w}_{r} satisfy a three-term recurrence of their own, so each follows from the two before it. The circuit computes each coefficient while its basis vector is still stored and immediately adds ξr​𝒘r\xi_{r}\boldsymbol{w}_{r} into a 48-symbol register, the locator register. When the walk ends, that register holds 𝝈\boldsymbol{\sigma}.

Breakdowns and scheduled repairs.

Lanczos removes the component of a vector 𝒗\boldsymbol{v} along a basis vector 𝒘\boldsymbol{w} by subtracting ρ​𝒘\rho\boldsymbol{w}, with ρ=(𝒘𝖳​𝒗)/(𝒘𝖳​𝒘)\rho=(\boldsymbol{w}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{v})/(\boldsymbol{w}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{w}). Over 𝔽64\mathbb{F}_{64}, however, a nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself, which leaves this quotient undefined. Block Lanczos repairs such a breakdown by treating the consecutive Krylov vectors 𝒘,A​𝒘,…,Ad−1​𝒘\boldsymbol{w},A\boldsymbol{w},\ldots,A^{d-1}\boldsymbol{w} as one block and removing the components along all of them at once. This is possible once their Gram matrix, the matrix of their inner products, is invertible:

Gd=[(Ai​𝒘)𝖳​(Aj​𝒘)]i,j=0d−1=[gi+j]i,j=0d−1,gk=𝒘𝖳​Ak​𝒘.G_{d}=\bigl[(A^{i}\boldsymbol{w})^{\mathsf{T}}(A^{j}\boldsymbol{w})\bigr]_{i,j=0}^{d-1}=\bigl[g_{i+j}\bigr]_{i,j=0}^{d-1},\qquad g_{k}=\boldsymbol{w}^{\mathsf{T}}A^{k}\boldsymbol{w}. (49)

We call dd the depth of the block. The circuit supports depths two and three.

A breakdown is rare, and the machinery that repairs it is expensive. An ordinary round of the walk costs 5,400 Toffolis; a round that can also repair at depth two costs 12,000, and one that can repair at depth three costs 17,000. A fixed circuit that repaired each breakdown where it occurred would carry this machinery in every round. The circuit instead concentrates it in scheduled repair rounds. It conditions the ordinary update on g0=𝒘𝖳​𝒘≠0g_{0}=\boldsymbol{w}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{w}\neq 0. This test is cheap: in characteristic 2, 𝒘𝖳​𝒘\boldsymbol{w}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{w} is the square of the sum of the components of 𝒘\boldsymbol{w}, which needs only CNOTs. On an input with g0=0g_{0}=0 the update gates do not act, and the walk state stays frozen until the next repair round, which forms the block and advances the walk past it in one step. The walk has 52 rounds, four more than the dimension, so that delayed inputs can finish. Of these, 17 carry repair machinery. An input that needs a deeper block, or that has not finished after 52 rounds, fails.

Ending and reversing the walk.

For a given input, the walk ends when g0=g1=g2=0g_{0}=g_{1}=g_{2}=0, because no block of depth up to three is then invertible. The circuit freezes the walk there and records the round, as the divstep circuit does (SI II.1). After the last round, it tests which of three cases holds and routes the corresponding vector into the locator register. If 𝒘=0\boldsymbol{w}=0, the Krylov vectors have become dependent, and the accumulated vector is the null vector. If 𝒘≠0\boldsymbol{w}\neq 0 and A​𝒘=0A\boldsymbol{w}=0, then 𝒘\boldsymbol{w} itself is a null vector. If A​𝒘≠0A\boldsymbol{w}\neq 0 and A2​𝒘=0A^{2}\boldsymbol{w}=0, then A​𝒘A\boldsymbol{w} is a null vector. An input in none of these cases fails.

After the phase scan described below, the circuit must undo the walk. It first measures the locator register in the XX basis. The walk built that register by adding multiples of basis vectors, so the reverse walk can correct the phase left by the measurement as it retraces the rounds: each addition becomes a set of controlled-ZZ gates conditioned on the measurement outcomes, at no Toffoli cost. The reverse walk recomputes most of the decisions of the forward walk, such as its zero tests, while the vectors they depend on are present. One decision per round cannot be recomputed in time: whether the round advanced the walk, which controls an exchange of the two stored basis vectors. The forward walk stores that decision in one history qubit per round, 52 in all, and the reverse walk clears them. The reverse walk uses 52,000 fewer Toffolis than the forward walk.

Error values.

The locator gives the possible error points, and the phase also needs the error values. The circuit uses two facts, both counterparts of the Reed–Solomon decoder (Table S2). First, there is an evaluator ω\omega whose coefficients are bilinear in the locator and the syndromes, as ω=σ​S\omega=\sigma S is for Reed–Solomon codes. Second, the error value at a simple zero of the locator is

ej=ω⁡(Pj)σ′​(Pj),σ′=∂xσ+x8​∂yσ,e_{j}=\frac{\omega(P_{j})}{\sigma^{\prime}(P_{j})},\qquad\sigma^{\prime}=\partial_{x}\sigma+x^{8}\partial_{y}\sigma, (50)

the counterpart of Forney’s formula (30). Here σ′\sigma^{\prime} is the derivative of the locator along the curve. Differentiating Equation 41 in characteristic 2 gives d​y=x8​d​xdy=x^{8}dx, so a step d​xdx along the curve changes σ\sigma by σ′​d​x\sigma^{\prime}\,dx. The evaluator is ω=σ​S^\omega=\sigma\widehat{S}, where S^\widehat{S} is the counterpart of the syndrome polynomial S⁡(z)S(z): a series whose leading coefficients, in decreasing weighted degree, are the 123 syndromes [51].

The locator comes from a 48-dimensional space and is not necessarily the minimal-degree locator. It can therefore also vanish at a point that carries no error, or have a repeated zero at an error point. At a point with no error, ω\omega vanishes as well and the point contributes nothing. At a repeated zero the quotient becomes 0/00/0. As in L’Hôpital’s rule, the error value then comes from the first few coefficients of the expansions of ω\omega and σ\sigma at that point, which we call local coefficients. The circuit supports repeated zeros up to multiplicity three.

Striped phase scan.

For a curve point PjP_{j}, write cjc_{j} for its six mask bits and eje_{j} for its error value. As in the Reed–Solomon decoder, the mask bits define μj∈𝔽64\mu_{j}\in\mathbb{F}_{64} with ⟨cj,ej⟩2=Tr𝔽64/𝔽2⁡(μj​ej)\langle c_{j},e_{j}\rangle_{2}=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{F}_{64}/\mathbb{F}_{2}}(\mu_{j}e_{j}), and part of the phase is linear in the syndromes and costs only ZZ gates. The residual constant μ~j\widetilde{\mu}_{j} vanishes at 128 points, which leaves 384 points to scan.

At each of these points the circuit needs three local coefficients of ω\omega. Computing ω\omega once and storing it would hold more than 100 field symbols through the whole scan. The circuit instead works in 24 stripes of 16 points. For each stripe it computes only the 16×3=4816\times 3=48 symbols that the stripe needs, uses them, and erases them by MBU at no Toffoli cost. The matching local coefficients of the locator are linear in its coefficient vector and cost only CNOTs.

Recomputing for every stripe is affordable only because ω\omega is cheap to form. A direct construction multiplies the expansion of S^\widehat{S} by σ\sigma coefficient by coefficient, which uses 2,452 field multiplications, or 37,000 Toffolis. The circuit uses evaluation–interpolation instead, as in Equation 46. One obstacle is that the syndromes give S^\widehat{S} only as the leading coefficients of an expansion, which cannot be evaluated at a curve point. The circuit therefore replaces S^\widehat{S} by a function that can be evaluated: a fraction h𝒔=n𝒔/qh_{\boldsymbol{s}}=n_{\boldsymbol{s}}/q of two polynomials in xx and yy, with a fixed denominator and a numerator that is linear in the syndromes 𝒔=(S0,…,S122)𝖳\boldsymbol{s}=(S_{0},\ldots,S_{122})^{\mathsf{T}}. The fraction is chosen so that its product with any locator agrees with σ​S^\sigma\widehat{S} in every coefficient that the scan uses. All products σ​h𝒔\sigma h_{\boldsymbol{s}} lie in a fixed 206-dimensional space, so their values at 206 suitably chosen curve points determine those coefficients, at 206×15=3,090206\times 15=3{,}090 Toffolis per stripe. The 24 stripes cost 74,000 Toffolis in total. This is more than the 37,000 Toffolis of one direct construction, but it avoids storing ω\omega.

At each point, the circuit then forms the phase bit Tr⁡(μ~j​ω/σ′)\operatorname{Tr}(\widetilde{\mu}_{j}\,\omega/\sigma^{\prime}) from the local coefficients. Division in 𝔽64\mathbb{F}_{64} is cheap: the circuit computes the inverse with arithmetic in the smaller field 𝔽8\mathbb{F}_{8}, and the whole computation costs 33 Toffolis per point.

On 100,000 random inputs, 30 produce the wrong sign. The circuit uses 930,000 Toffolis and 2,395 qubits, for a T​QTQ-cost of 2.2×1092.2\times 10^{9}. Relative to the Feng–Rao baseline, this reduces the Toffoli count by 110×110\times, the qubit count by 81×81\times, and the T​QTQ-cost by 9,100×9{,}100\times.

II Prime-field modular inversion

We benchmark modular inversion within a complete arithmetic circuit: point addition on an elliptic curve over a 256-bit prime field. Each point on this curve is a pair of integers (x,y)(x,y) satisfying the curve equation

y2≡x3+7(modp),y^{2}\equiv x^{3}+7\pmod{p}, (51)

where p=2256−232−977p=2^{256}-2^{32}-977 is a 256-bit prime number. The curve defines point addition, an operation that combines two points PP and QQ into a third point R=P+QR=P+Q on the same curve (note that this addition is not the usual coordinate-wise addition). Geometrically, one draws the line through PP and QQ, finds its third intersection with the curve, and reflects that point across the horizontal axis. Algebraically, for the inputs considered here, with Qx≠PxQ_{x}\neq P_{x}, one first computes the slope

λ≡(Qy−Py)​(Qx−Px)−1(modp),\lambda\equiv(Q_{y}-P_{y})(Q_{x}-P_{x})^{-1}\pmod{p}, (52)

where (Qx−Px)−1(Q_{x}-P_{x})^{-1} denotes the inverse modulo pp. The coordinates of the sum are then

Rx=λ2−Px−Qx,Ry=λ⁡(Px−Rx)−Py.R_{x}=\lambda^{2}-P_{x}-Q_{x},\qquad R_{y}=\lambda(P_{x}-R_{x})-P_{y}. (53)

We study the reversible point adder [52]: given an input point PP and another, classically supplied point QQ, it performs

|P⟩⟼|P+Q⟩.\ket{P}\longmapsto\ket{P+Q}. (54)

The modular inverse required by Equation 52 is the dominant cost of point addition: once the slope λ\lambda is known, the remaining coordinate updates require only a fixed sequence of relatively cheap modular additions and multiplications. In contrast, modular inversion follows a long input-dependent sequence of arithmetic transitions, which the circuit must later recover to reverse the computation and clear its ancillas.

Prior point-addition constructions [8, 38] use the binary greatest common divisor (gcd) algorithm for modular inversion. The connection between gcd and inversion comes from expressing the gcd in terms of the original inputs. Because pp is prime and w=Qx−Px≠0w=Q_{x}-P_{x}\neq 0, there are integers α\alpha and β\beta such that gcd⁡(p,w)=1=α​p+β​w\gcd(p,w)=1=\alpha p+\beta w. Reducing this identity modulo pp gives β​w≡1\beta w\equiv 1, so β≡w−1(modp)\beta\equiv w^{-1}\pmod{p}. The extended binary-gcd algorithm finds these coefficients by tracking expressions for the two current values uu and vv as integer combinations of pp and ww. Binary gcd rests on two elementary identities. If uu is even and vv is odd, then gcd⁡(u,v)=gcd⁡(u/2,v)\gcd(u,v)=\gcd(u/2,v); if uu and vv are both odd, then, for u>vu>v, gcd⁡(u,v)=gcd⁡((u−v)/2,v)\gcd(u,v)=\gcd((u-v)/2,v). Applying these identities symmetrically gives the reduction

(u,v)⟼{(u/2,v)for ​u​ even,(u,v/2)for ​v​ even,((u−v)/2,v)for ​u>v,u,v​ odd,(u,(v−u)/2)for ​v>u,u,v​ odd.(u,v)\longmapsto\begin{cases}(u/2,v)&\text{for }u\text{ even},\\ (u,v/2)&\text{for }v\text{ even},\\ ((u-v)/2,v)&\text{for }u>v,\quad u,v\text{ odd},\\ (u,(v-u)/2)&\text{for }v>u,\quad u,v\text{ odd}.\end{cases} (55)

Each case preserves the gcd and makes one value smaller.

Making this reduction reversible is difficult because its control flow is input-dependent: which line of Equation 55 applies changes from one step to the next, and the reduced pair does not in general reveal which line produced it. A quantum circuit therefore cannot simply run the reduction backward to restore its input and clear its workspace; it must preserve enough information to identify each step. The prior constructions do so using the dialog introduced by Khattar et al. [13]. The direct approach would update the coefficients that become α\alpha and β\beta alongside the two values throughout the reduction. The dialog avoids holding these growing coefficients in memory. Its first pass updates only the pair being reduced and records a compact symbol identifying each subtraction, swap, and halving choice. A second pass replays the same transformations to construct the required coefficient. Initializing this replay from the numerator a=Qy−Pya=Q_{y}-P_{y} produces a​β=a​w−1modpa\beta=aw^{-1}\bmod p directly, without ever storing w−1w^{-1} in a separate register. The simple binary updates and the replay trick reduce the gate count, but the complete dialog record requires hundreds of additional qubits. Table S3 compares these constructions with the two circuits reported below.

II.1 Divsteps

Rather than reorganize the binary-gcd constructions above, the search finds a new reversible prime-field inversion architecture built on divsteps [15, 53]. In the divstep recurrence of Equation 6, a small signed counter zz, called the half delta, replaces the repeated magnitude comparisons in Equation 55: the sign of zz and the parity of one value alone determine the next update. We call the choice of update at a step its decision. Appendix A proves that every decision can be computed exactly from the registers as they stand after the step. When a decision is cheap to decode, the circuit decodes it from the updated state. Otherwise, the circuit stores the decision as a single bit on a fixed-size history stack. We call the sequence of divsteps for one input a walk. The point adder uses this inversion twice, once to form the slope λ\lambda and once to erase it after the coordinate update. Each use runs a forward walk and a reverse walk, for four walks in total.

Unlike the quotient-based extended Euclidean algorithm (EEA) of SI II.2, which divides one remainder by the other at every iteration, a divstep never computes a multi-bit quotient or adds a multiple of one full register to another. A divstep walk needs more steps than the quotient-based EEA needs divisions, but each step is much cheaper. Reversible divsteps were previously developed over binary fields and polynomial rings [54, 13]. There, each step shrinks the polynomial pair by one coefficient, and the freed space can hold that step’s record. Integer divsteps free no such fixed space, so a stored history costs additional qubits. To our knowledge, this is the first reversible divstep inversion circuit over a prime field.

We recall the notation of the main text. The walk state is (z,f,g,fv,gv)(z,f,g,f_{v},g_{v}), and each step applies one of the three updates in Equation 6. Two bits label the update: ss records whether the step swaps the roles of ff and gg, and bb records whether the incoming gg is odd. To run a step backward, the circuit must know ss and bb, and the updated state does not hold them explicitly. Cheap tests on a few bits of the updated state recover ss at every step and bb at about two thirds of the steps. We call the remaining decisions ambiguous. Each ambiguous decision has a depth jj, the number of trailing zero bits of the updated coefficient fv′f_{v}^{\prime}, and we write fv′=2j​qf_{v}^{\prime}=2^{j}q with qq odd. A swap followed by a run of ambiguous decisions is an excursion, and the depth counts the steps of the excursion so far, with the swap as step 1. The cost of a depth-jj decoder grows with jj. The cutoff jstorej_{\mathrm{store}} is the depth from which the circuit stops decoding: it decodes an ambiguous decision at depth j<jstorej<j_{\mathrm{store}} and stores one at depth j≥jstorej\geq j_{\mathrm{store}}.

The cutoff jstorej_{\mathrm{store}} trades qubits for Toffolis: a higher cutoff decodes more and stores less. At jstore=0j_{\mathrm{store}}=0, the circuit uses only the cheap tests and stores every remaining decision, requiring 198 history qubits for the 533-step schedule and 1,065 qubits in total. The discovered circuit chooses the intermediate cutoff jstore=5j_{\mathrm{store}}=5: it decodes depths two through four with the rules given below. Storing only the deeper decisions shrinks the history stack from 198 to 60 qubits. At the low-qubit extreme, jstore=9j_{\mathrm{store}}=9 decodes through j=8j=8 and reserves 24 history qubits. Varying the cutoff and the workspace produces a family of circuits that spans from 3.6 million Toffolis and 1,031 qubits to 7.9 million Toffolis and 893 qubits; an additional higher-qubit configuration uses 3.3 million Toffolis and 1,191 qubits.

Branch decoders.

A forward step computes bb from the parity of gg and uses it to control the update. After the update, gg no longer holds that parity, so the step is left with bb in a qubit of its own. Uncomputing bb there would require the decoder on the forward walk as well. The forward step instead disposes of bb in one of two ways. If the decision is ambiguous at depth j≥jstorej\geq j_{\mathrm{store}}, the step pushes bb onto the history stack. Otherwise, the step removes bb by MBU: it measures bb in the XX basis. The measurement frees the qubit but leaves a phase that depends on bb and on the measurement outcome.

The reverse walk is the uncomputation of the forward walk. Once the circuit has used the inverse, it undoes the forward steps in the opposite order, which restores ww and returns the walk registers to zero. The matching reverse step obtains bb again, either by popping the stack or by applying the tests and decoders to the updated state. It applies the phase correction for the measurement outcome and uses bb to choose which update to undo. The restored gg then holds bb as its parity, so a CNOT from the low bit of gg clears it. Decoders therefore appear only in reverse steps. A walk that stores more decisions than the stack holds overflows it and fails.

The decoders evaluate the second form of Equation A11, b=bitj−1⁡(p​(f′​q)−1mod2j)b=\operatorname{bit}_{j-1}(p(f^{\prime}q)^{-1}\bmod 2^{j}). Both f′f^{\prime} and qq are odd, so the depth-jj decoder is a Boolean function of 2​(j−1)2(j-1) bits. Write fi=f′​[i]f_{i}=f^{\prime}[i] and qi=q⁡[i]=fv′​[j+i]q_{i}=q[i]=f_{v}^{\prime}[j+i] for 1≤i<j1\leq i<j, where u⁡[i]u[i] is bit ii of uu. For the prime pp of Equation 51, the decoders at depths two through five are

j=2:b\displaystyle j=2:\quad b =1⊕f1⊕q1,\displaystyle=1\oplus f_{1}\oplus q_{1}, (56a)
j=3:b\displaystyle j=3:\quad b =1⊕f2⊕q2,\displaystyle=1\oplus f_{2}\oplus q_{2}, (56b)
j=4:b\displaystyle j=4:\quad b =1⊕f1⊕f2⊕f3⊕q1⊕q2⊕q3⊕(f1⊕f2)​(q1⊕q2),\displaystyle=1\oplus f_{1}\oplus f_{2}\oplus f_{3}\oplus q_{1}\oplus q_{2}\oplus q_{3}\oplus(f_{1}\oplus f_{2})(q_{1}\oplus q_{2}), (56c)
j=5:b\displaystyle j=5:\quad b =f3⊕f4⊕q3⊕q4⊕Mf⊕Mq⊕f1​q1⊕f2​q3⊕f3​q2⊕f3​q3\displaystyle=f_{3}\oplus f_{4}\oplus q_{3}\oplus q_{4}\oplus M_{f}\oplus M_{q}\oplus f_{1}q_{1}\oplus f_{2}q_{3}\oplus f_{3}q_{2}\oplus f_{3}q_{3}
⊕Mf​(q1⊕q2)⊕(f1⊕f2)​Mq,\displaystyle\quad\oplus M_{f}(q_{1}\oplus q_{2})\oplus(f_{1}\oplus f_{2})M_{q}, (56d)

where Mf=f1​f2⊕f1​f3⊕f2​f3M_{f}=f_{1}f_{2}\oplus f_{1}f_{3}\oplus f_{2}f_{3} is the majority of f1,f2,f3f_{1},f_{2},f_{3} and MqM_{q} is the majority of q1,q2,q3q_{1},q_{2},q_{3}. Written out as sums of products, these four rules have 3, 3, 11, and 26 terms. The decoders at depths six, seven, and eight have 79, 268, and 1,092 terms. The growth reflects Equation A13: the deciding bit sits above the bit of every earlier decision in the excursion, and the multiplication by q−1q^{-1} carries through all of them.

The circuit implements equivalent forms of these rules. The determinant identity of Equation A3 fixes gv′mod2jg_{v}^{\prime}\bmod 2^{j} once f′f^{\prime} is known, so a decoder may read a bit of gv′g_{v}^{\prime} in place of bits of f′f^{\prime}. The depth-two decoder is Equation A14, which costs two Toffolis. At depths three and four, the rule is an XOR of bits of qq, with no products, once f′mod16f^{\prime}\bmod 16 is fixed. From depth five on, the rule contains products of bits of qq.

These rules explain where the cutoff sits. Every reverse step must contain the decoder for every depth below jstorej_{\mathrm{store}}, whether or not that step needs it. Each decoder is conditioned on a flag marking the depth, so each term that reads a register bit costs at least one Toffoli. The benefit shrinks as the cost grows: among ambiguous decisions in sampled walks, 50.1%50.1\% occur at depth two, 25.0%25.0\% at depth three, 12.5%12.5\% at depth four, and 12.4%12.4\% at all greater depths. Beyond depth four, each further depth roughly triples the number of terms and removes half as much history as the depth before it.

Early stopping.

A walk terminates when gg reaches zero: at that point f=±1f=\pm 1 and the inverse can be read from fvf_{v}. Different inputs terminate at different steps, typically between steps 505 and 530 (Figure 3(b)), but the circuit runs a fixed schedule of 533 steps. The steps after termination must leave the state unchanged. Left alone, the recurrence would treat g=0g=0 as an even value, so it would keep doubling fvf_{v} and incrementing zz until both outgrow their registers.

The circuit therefore freezes a terminated walk. Each forward step tests whether g=0g=0. On the first step where the test succeeds, the circuit sets a one-qubit frozen flag, and from then on the flag disables every update. The reverse walk must clear the flag at that same step. A frozen state looks identical at every later step, so the state alone cannot reveal when the walk froze. The circuit writes the step index into a small register when it sets the flag. Each reverse step compares the register with its own index, and a match clears both the flag and the register.

This machinery costs Toffolis at every step: a test that every bit of gg is zero, and one more control on every update. The test is most expensive in the early steps, where gg is widest and termination is least likely. The first 498 steps omit the test, the flag, and the flag’s controls. A walk that terminates within those steps fails. The measured probability is 1.4×10−61.4\times 10^{-6} per inversion, and Table S4 uses 3×10−63\times 10^{-6} as an upper bound.

A walk whose counter zz outgrows its register also fails, with probability 9×10−89\times 10^{-8} per inversion; the two events give the early-stopping row of Table S4.

Removing the power-of-two scale.

At termination, f​fvff_{v} equals the desired inverse times 2t2^{t}, where tt counts the active steps, those before the walk freezes (Proposition A.2):

f​fv≡2t​w−1(modp).ff_{v}\equiv 2^{t}w^{-1}\pmod{p}. (57)

The stopping time tt depends on the input, so different branches of a superposition carry different scales. Classical implementations avoid this by running a fixed number of steps, which makes the scale a known constant; the circuit instead freezes when g=0g=0. A direct approach would count tt in a register, apply a multiplication by 2−t2^{-t} controlled on that register, and then uncompute the count.

The circuit avoids this count. It sets r=a​f​fv≡2t​a​w−1(modp)r=aff_{v}\equiv 2^{t}aw^{-1}\pmod{p}, where aa is the field value to be multiplied by the inverse. For the slope of Equation 52, w=Qx−Pxw=Q_{x}-P_{x} is the denominator and a=Qy−Pya=Q_{y}-P_{y} is the numerator. The reverse walk then undoes exactly tt active steps, and the frozen flag marks which steps are active. The circuit attaches one modular halving of rr to each active reverse step: r↦r/2r\mapsto r/2 if rr is even and r↦(r+p)/2r\mapsto(r+p)/2 otherwise. After the reverse walk, r=a​w−1r=aw^{-1}, the input ww is restored, and no record of tt remains.

Step-dependent qubit reuse.

A naïve layout would give each of the four signed integers f,g,fv,gvf,g,f_{v},g_{v} its own permanent 256-bit register, consuming 1,024 qubits before the counter, controls, or history stack are included. These registers do not all need their full capacity simultaneously: as the walk progresses, ff and gg need progressively fewer bits, while fvf_{v} and gvg_{v} need more. Each step halves gg, and swaps alternate which value plays the role of gg. Each step also doubles a coefficient. The packed Euclidean construction of Luo et al. [40] and its specialization in SI II.2 use the same fact: a shrinking remainder and growing coefficient occupy opposite ends of one register, as visualized in Figure S2(a). The discovered divstep circuit applies this idea to f,g,fv,gvf,g,f_{v},g_{v} using two 256-qubit registers rather than four: gg and fvf_{v} share the register that initially holds ww, and ff and gvg_{v} share the other. Within each register, the growing coefficient claims positions vacated by its shrinking partner. The width and position of every value at every step are fixed when the circuit is built. A walk in which a value outgrows its assigned width fails; this event is the integer-size limit in Table S4.

Fused coordinate arithmetic.

For the remaining coordinate arithmetic, the circuit does not call general multiplication, squaring, or reduction circuits. It adds each term of the coordinate formulas straight into the register that needs it. For the square, the coordinate update needs λ2\lambda^{2} only while forming RxR_{x}. Splitting λ=λ0+2128​λ1\lambda=\lambda_{0}+2^{128}\lambda_{1} gives

λ2=λ02+2129​λ0​λ1+2256​λ12(modp).\lambda^{2}=\lambda_{0}^{2}+2^{129}\lambda_{0}\lambda_{1}+2^{256}\lambda_{1}^{2}\pmod{p}. (58)

This expresses the 256-bit square as three products involving only 128-bit halves. The circuit adds them one at a time directly into the coordinate register and clears each temporary product before computing the next. It therefore avoids both a register for the completed square and the second full multiplication of the usual approach, which computes the square, copies it, and uncomputes it.

The remaining coordinate products exploit the special form of the prime pp. Since

2256≡232+977(modp),2^{256}\equiv 2^{32}+977\pmod{p}, (59)

the circuit can replace any bits above bit 255 with a small correction to the low bits instead of performing a general modular reduction. The circuit applies this correction while it forms each product, so it never holds a complete product that it must later clear.

We require the exact map in Equation 54, including its phase and the return of every ancilla to zero, except on at most a 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} fraction of inputs 33 3 We draw PP and QQ independently and nearly uniformly from the points of the curve, omitting the cases on which the affine formulas are incomplete.. The 16-bit-window algorithm of Babbush et al. [8] invokes the point adder 28 times; by a union bound, the failure budget adds less than 0.6%0.6\% retry overhead.

The four divstep walks use 2.5 million Toffolis, 63%63\% of the circuit. The field multiplications around the walks use 1.4 million, 35%35\% of the circuit. The fused square and the coordinate additions use the remaining 0.10 million. The 935-qubit peak occurs during a walk. The algebraic identities behind the recurrence, branch decoders, fused square, and sparse-prime reductions are exact. Failures arise only from the finite stopping-time, integer-size, history, carry, and comparison limits.

Reducing modulo the sparse prime adds a short constant, 232+9772^{32}+977 or a small multiple of it, to the low end of a 256-bit register. In principle the carry from this addition can travel up the whole register. In practice it rarely travels far, because it keeps moving only while the bits above it are ones. The circuit therefore propagates each such carry through only the low 58 bits (60 in the fused square) and drops any carry that would go further. This happens with probability about 2−262^{-26} per reduction. The comparison limit uses the same idea: to decide whether a modular addition overflowed, the circuit compares only the top 27 bits of the two operands, which gives the wrong answer only when those bits all agree. Table S4 collects all contributions 44 4 An exact worst-case analysis guarantees that every nonzero input modulo pp terminates within 590 divsteps, compared with the circuit’s 533-step schedule [36]. Within 533 scheduled steps, an excursion whose swap fires at counter value z=Dz=D consumes 2​D+12D+1 steps and stores at most D−3D-3 decisions, so a walk can store at most (533−1)/2−3=263(533-1)/2-3=263 decisions. The hatching in Figure 3(b) extends to this ceiling.; each entry is the per-use failure rate times the number of uses in one point addition. Among 100,000 tests of the full circuit, four fail.

II.2 Specialized Euclidean construction

This subsection reports a second discovered circuit, at the low-qubit end of the Toffoli–qubit frontier (Table S3): 843 qubits against 935 for the divstep circuit, at about five times the Toffoli count. Here the search does not find a new inversion algorithm. It starts from the space-efficient Euclidean point adder of Luo et al. [40], which we rebuilt as a complete circuit, and specializes its schedule for the prime pp. The schedule is the fixed list of steps, and of bit positions within each step, that the circuit runs. Our reconstruction, the baseline below, uses 69.5 million Toffolis and 838 qubits. The discovered specialization uses 843 qubits while reducing the Toffoli count to 20.5 million, a factor of 3.43.4. We use the same inputs and outputs, input distribution, and failure budget as above.

To invert ww modulo pp, the EEA starts from r−1=pr_{-1}=p and r0=wr_{0}=w and computes

ai=⌊ri−1ri⌋,ri+1=ri−1−ai​ri.a_{i}=\left\lfloor\frac{r_{i-1}}{r_{i}}\right\rfloor,\qquad r_{i+1}=r_{i-1}-a_{i}r_{i}. (60)

Alongside the remainders, it maintains coefficients t−1=0,t0=1t_{-1}=0,t_{0}=1, with ti+1=ti−1+ai​tit_{i+1}=t_{i-1}+a_{i}t_{i}. When a remainder reaches one, the corresponding coefficient gives the modular inverse up to sign.

Each iteration of Equation 60 is an integer division. The quotient aia_{i} of the two current remainders drives both updates: the remainder update subtracts aia_{i} copies of one remainder from the other, and the coefficient update adds aia_{i} copies of one coefficient to the other. The quotients depend on the input and vary in size, so the circuit must compute each one coherently before it can apply it. It performs each division by binary long division. We call one elementary move of this division a step; a division whose quotient has ℓ\ell bits takes 4​ℓ4\ell steps. The total over an inversion depends on the input and is at most 1,616 for the prime pp, so the baseline schedules 1,616 steps.

The baseline circuit exploits the fact that the remainders rir_{i} shrink as the coefficients tit_{i} grow. It stores a remainder and a coefficient from opposite ends of the same register, and stores the succeeding pair in a second such register. We call values that share a register in this way packed. Four short counters record where the four values begin and end. The circuit processes these packed values by scanning across their possible bit positions. At each position, it uses the counters to decide whether that bit belongs to the value currently being processed; we call this check a counter test. If it does, the circuit performs the required one-bit arithmetic; otherwise it does nothing. The fixed circuit must include this test and arithmetic for every position that any input could require, even though a particular input uses only a much smaller range of positions.

Each step runs several scans, one each for the remainder update, the coefficient update, and the rearrangement of the packed values. The path that the boundary between a remainder and a coefficient traces during an inversion is the input’s Euclidean walk.

Each use of the inversion performs an in-place division or multiplication. For the slope, a forward pass replaces ww by its inverse, one multiplication forms the quotient in an accumulator, an XX-basis measurement erases the old numerator, and the reverse pass restores ww. The second inversion runs the same sequence in the opposite order to erase the slope. Every step consists of in-place reversible operations on the packed registers and counters, so the reverse pass is the inverse circuit and needs no stored history. By contrast, the divstep circuit must recover a decision at every step.

The discovered circuit keeps the baseline’s packed register layout and reduces the cost of its schedule mainly in three ways. First, it omits scan positions that inputs rarely use. Second, it removes selected counter tests. Third, it recompiles the scans of a step together so that they share intermediate results. The first two changes fail on rare inputs, which count against the 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} failure budget per point addition. The third is exact.

Fitted windows and the schedule cut.

The baseline circuit includes arithmetic at every bit position required by its worst-case bounds. Most inputs occupy a much narrower range at each step. The specialized schedule therefore replaces each worst-case range with a fitted window: a range chosen separately for each step and fitted to the positions that sampled walks use. The same fit shortens the schedule from the worst-case 1,616 steps to 1,432 steps; we call this shortening the schedule cut. Figure S2(b) shows how closely sampled walks concentrate within the windows, compared with the worst-case bounds.

Test-free positions.

A fitted window still leaves a counter test at every position inside it, and a counter test is expensive. In the baseline, a position whose arithmetic is conditioned on a counter costs about ten Toffolis, several times the cost of the arithmetic alone. Where every sampled input uses a position at a given step, the schedule marks the position test-free, and the circuit performs its arithmetic unconditionally. Counter tests remain at the other positions inside the window, near the moving boundaries of the values. On an input that does not use a test-free position, the unconditional arithmetic produces a wrong result. The two approximations remove different costs. A fitted window deletes both the test and the arithmetic at the positions outside it. A test-free position keeps the arithmetic and deletes the test. Figure S2(c) shows the resulting per-step cost.

Merged scans and measured carries.

The baseline circuit compiles the scans within a step separately, so neighboring scans repeat some of the same comparisons and compute some of the same control bits. Compiling the complete step as one operation removes this repetition; we call this change merged scans. The clearest instance is the remainder update. The comparison that decides whether a subtraction applies and the subtraction itself run over the same two remainders, and the baseline compiles them as two passes. The discovered circuit merges them into one compare-and-subtract scan whose intermediate bits serve both operations. It then erases those bits by measurement, which needs no Toffolis, instead of uncomputing them. The baseline also shifts a register’s contents, by an amount that depends on the input, as the values change size. The discovered circuit renumbers the positions instead of moving the qubits, which costs no gates. In the additions that remain, a carry that only one position needs is likewise erased by measurement (measured carries). These changes are exact.

Multiplier arithmetic.

The coordinate update also requires modular squaring and multiplication. The discovered circuit specializes these operations to the sparse prime pp. The exact part of the rewrite, the sparse-prime multipliers, uses the fold of Equation 59, as in SI II.1. The approximate part, the truncated multipliers, limits how far a carry propagates and how many bits a comparison inspects.

Figure S2(d) shows the cumulative Toffoli reduction. The two inversions, including their forward and reverse passes, together account for 98%98\% of the Toffolis.

We estimate the failure probability empirically. Across 10 million sampled walks, 72 use a position outside a fitted window and 258 do not use a test-free position, a combined rate of about 6.6×10−56.6\times 10^{-5} per point addition. The schedule cut adds 1.3×10−51.3\times 10^{-5}, and the truncated multipliers add at most 2×10−62\times 10^{-6}. The total is about 8×10−58\times 10^{-5} per point addition. Among 100,000 tests of the full circuit, four fail.

III Numerical function evaluation

Elementary-function evaluation has been a central problem in numerical computing since the earliest mathematical software libraries. The routines conventionally collected in libm, the mathematical-function library supplied by C and Unix systems, evaluate roots, exponentials, logarithms, and trigonometric functions by combining range reduction, table lookup, polynomial approximation, and iterative refinement [57]. These functions also appear throughout quantum algorithms. They determine controlled rotation angles in quantum linear-systems algorithms [58, 12], set interaction phases in real-space Hamiltonian simulation [59, 60], and enter the amplitudes prepared for Hamiltonian simulation [4].

These classical techniques cannot simply be ported into coherent quantum circuits. Data-dependent choices must be compiled into a fixed gate sequence, and all temporary state must ultimately be returned to |0⟩\ket{0}. The latter reversibility constraint is particularly costly for numerical routines because many classical methods proceed through a long sequence of large, high-precision intermediate values. An ordinary implementation can overwrite each value and reuse the same storage as soon as the next value is formed. A reversible implementation must instead retain enough information to reconstruct the overwritten value, or recompute it when clearing the circuit. Consequently, composing individually efficient routines can accumulate many large live registers and may require running the complete computation backward after its result has been consumed. Iterative Newton-style methods repeatedly replace one full-precision estimate with another, so their reversible implementations carry large intermediate registers through every step [61]. Floating-point representations add exponent bits to every such register to track a wide range of magnitudes [62]. The approximation, fixed-point representation, and uncomputation schedule therefore become inseparable parts of circuit design [12].

We consider three numerical subroutines: Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd (HHL) rotation-angle evaluation (arcsin\arcsin), Coulomb-potential evaluation (1/‖x‖21/\sqrt{\|x\|^{2}}), and Gaussian evaluation (e−x2e^{-x^{2}}) [58, 59, 2]. Each implements an additive fixed-point map |x⟩​|k⟩↦|x⟩​|k+f~​(x)⟩\ket{x}\ket{k}\mapsto\ket{x}\ket{k+\widetilde{f}(x)}, with a uniform error bound over its promised domain 55 5 Throughout this section, round denotes nearest-integer rounding, with half-integer ties away from zero. Because each result is accumulated modulo 2n2^{n} in an nn-bit register, we measure the error between aa and bb by the circular distance minm∈ℤ⁡|a−b+m​2n|\min_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}|a-b+m2^{n}|, so that values that differ only by wraparound count as close. Behavior outside the promised domain is unrestricted.. The additive form serves both common uses of the result. An ordinary accumulator kk holds the value for later bitwise-controlled operations, while a phase-gradient accumulator converts the addition directly into a phase.

Our baselines use the piecewise-polynomial construction of Häner, Roetteler, and Svore (HRS) [12]. HRS partitions the domain, fits a low-degree polynomial on each interval, and coherently loads the selected polynomial’s coefficients. It evaluates the polynomial in general fixed-point arithmetic by Horner’s rule, which uses one multiplication per degree. It adds the result to the output and reverses the computation to clear its temporary registers. Its cost has four sources: locating an interval with arbitrary boundaries; the wide multiplications of the Horner polynomial-evaluation stage; the registers that hold intermediate products and the polynomial value; and the reverse pass that erases the loaded coefficients. For each task we tune the polynomial degree, fixed-point format, and published recomputation trade-offs, and widen each interval until it reaches the error bound. We then use the complete gate-level implementation with the lowest T​QTQ-cost.

The three discovered circuits still implement piecewise-polynomial approximations. They keep the HRS approximation family but reorganize it for reversible execution, addressing the four costs in turn. They choose finer partitions whose intervals can be identified from the input bits. No comparison is then needed, and a polynomial of lower degree on fewer input bits suffices: the HHL and Gaussian circuits replace cubics by quadratics, and the Coulomb circuit replaces quadratics by lines. Where the intervals differ in width, as in the HHL circuit, a rearrangement of the input bits maps them into one shared local coordinate, so that one arithmetic kernel serves every interval. This is the conditional routing of the main text: a cheap, interval-dependent rearrangement of the data surrounds one shared kernel. The arithmetic accumulates directly into its destination, avoiding registers for full products and for the function value. MBU (Methods) then clears the loaded coefficients without reversing the lookup.

One supporting technique makes these choices safe. An offline search fits the coefficients to the exact quantized and truncated integer computation that the circuit performs, rather than rounding an ideal real-valued approximation afterward. Coefficient widths, omitted product columns, shifts, truncation, and rounding therefore share one end-to-end error budget.

All three circuits use these techniques. They differ in how the input reaches the arithmetic. The HHL circuit, which we describe in full, uses intervals of unequal width and cyclically shifts the input bits into a shared coordinate. The Coulomb circuit first builds the squared distance and normalizes it. The Gaussian circuit folds its input onto the nonnegative axis, prunes its lookup, and reuses coefficient qubits.

III.1 HHL rotation angle

After phase estimation, HHL applies an eigenvalue-dependent rotation whose angle is θ=arcsin⁡(C/λ~)\theta=\arcsin(C/\widetilde{\lambda}); conditioning on the rotated ancilla reweights each eigencomponent by 1/λ~1/\widetilde{\lambda} [58]. We take C=1/2C=1/2 and represent the eigenvalue estimate by a 21-bit integer XX, with x=X/216∈[1,32)x=X/2^{16}\in[1,32). The circuit adds the 33-bit angle

f⁡(X)=𝚛𝚘𝚞𝚗𝚍⁡(232​arcsin⁡(215X))f(X)=\mathtt{round}\!\left(2^{32}\arcsin\!\left(\frac{2^{15}}{X}\right)\right) (61)

to an accumulator kk. We require error below 10−710^{-7} radians throughout the domain.

The tuned HRS baseline uses cubic fits on 35 intervals and general 44-bit fixed-point arithmetic. It meets the error bound with 16,000 Toffolis and 300 qubits. Locating the interval requires coherent comparisons against arbitrary boundaries, and each evaluation performs three multiplications on 44-bit numbers.

The discovered circuit restructures this dataflow with three transformations, illustrated in Figure S3.

Power-of-two-aligned intervals.

The function arcsin⁡(1/(2​x))\arcsin(1/(2x)) changes rapidly near x=1x=1 and progressively more slowly as xx increases. An arbitrary adaptive partition could follow this variation, but reversibly locating one of its intervals would require comparisons against general boundaries. The discovered circuit instead uses narrow intervals near x=1x=1 and wider ones where the function is flatter, while restricting every interval to the power-of-two-aligned, or dyadic, form [L,L+2b)[L,L+2^{b}) with LL a multiple of 2b2^{b}. We call such an interval a leaf, because these intervals are the leaves of a binary tree over the input bits. The leading bits of the input then determine the leaf.

Because selection is cheap, a much finer partition is affordable: the circuit uses 345 intervals of widths 282^{8} through 2152^{15}, whereas the baseline uses 35 arbitrary intervals. The finer partition simplifies the arithmetic in two ways. A quadratic suffices instead of the baseline cubic, reducing the number of multiplications, and each polynomial depends only on the narrow local displacement δ=X−L\delta=X-L, reducing its operand widths. A uniform partition at the finest width would require 7,936 intervals (Figure S3(b)), so the dyadic tree obtains these benefits without paying for uniformly fine resolution.

Shared local coordinate.

After selecting a leaf, a conventional polynomial-evaluation stage would form δ=X−L\delta=X-L and rescale it according to the leaf width, requiring arithmetic and temporary storage. Moreover, leaves of different widths initially present differently scaled inputs to the polynomial-evaluation stage. The circuit replaces this coordinate arithmetic with an in-place cyclic shift of the input bits. For X=L+δX=L+\delta in a width-2b2^{b} leaf, cyclically shifting the low 15 bits produces

d=215−b​δ+cL.d=2^{15-b}\delta+c_{L}. (62)

The varying bits δ\delta move to a common scale, while the fixed leaf bits wrap around to form cLc_{L}. Because cLc_{L} is constant within the leaf, the offline fit absorbs it into the coefficients. Thus every leaf feeds the same 15-bit polynomial-evaluation stage without subtraction, arithmetic rescaling, or a coordinate register (Figure S3(b)). For example, in a width-2122^{12} leaf, the low 15 bits consist of three bits fixed by the leaf followed by the 12 varying bits of δ\delta. Shifting those bits cyclically left by three places produces d=23​δ+cLd=2^{3}\delta+c_{L}.

Narrow direct accumulation.

For each leaf, the coefficient table defines the integer quadratic

qL​(d)=g0−d⁡(g1−g2​d),q_{L}(d)=g_{0}-d(g_{1}-g_{2}d), (63)

with intercept g0g_{0}, slope g1g_{1}, and curvature g2g_{2}. A general Horner polynomial-evaluation stage multiplies large fixed-point numbers, retains work registers for those products, and materializes the polynomial value before adding it to the output. The shared polynomial-evaluation stage instead consumes the selected coefficients in place. It first overwrites the loaded slope g1g_{1} with the inner Horner value, then accumulates the outer product directly into kk:

t←g1−g2​d(stored over g1),k←k+g0−d​t.t\leftarrow g_{1}-g_{2}d\quad\text{(stored over $g_{1}$)},\qquad k\leftarrow k+g_{0}-dt. (64)

No separate register ever holds the completed polynomial or either full product.

The products themselves are also truncated: the circuit omits the low-order partial-product columns whose combined effect stays inside the error budget. The offline search fits the integer coefficients gig_{i} to the exact updates in Equation 64, including the truncated columns.

The worst-case error over all inputs is 9.95×10−89.95\times 10^{-8} radians. The circuit uses 1,348 Toffolis and 115 qubits, for a T​QTQ-cost of 160,000. Relative to the tuned HRS baseline, this reduces the Toffoli count by 12×12\times, the qubit count by 2.6×2.6\times, and the T​QTQ-cost by 32×32\times.

III.2 Coulomb potential

Real-space simulation repeatedly applies phases proportional to the inverse distance between particle pairs [59, 60]. For distinct points ri,rj∈{0,…,255}3r_{i},r_{j}\in\{0,\ldots,255\}^{3}, our circuit adds

F⁡(ri,rj)=𝚛𝚘𝚞𝚗𝚍⁡(224∑c∈{x,y,z}(ri,c−rj,c)2)F(r_{i},r_{j})=\mathtt{round}\!\left(\frac{2^{24}}{\sqrt{\sum_{c\in\{x,y,z\}}(r_{i,c}-r_{j,c})^{2}}}\right) (65)

to a 25-bit accumulator kk. We require error below 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} in the inverse distance. The tuned HRS baseline normalizes the squared distance and evaluates quadratics over 16 intervals, using 6,355 Toffolis and 252 qubits. The discovered circuit instead builds the squared distance in a single accumulation, replaces the quadratics by a finer table of lines, and erases that larger lookup cheaply.

Direct squared-distance accumulation.

The inverse-square-root approximation begins from the exact squared distance d2=∑c(ri,c−rj,c)2d^{2}=\sum_{c}(r_{i,c}-r_{j,c})^{2}. A conventional implementation would form the three coordinate squares in separate product registers and then add them. The discovered circuit instead adds the partial products of all three squares directly into one accumulator. This yields d2d^{2} exactly, without three product registers or a separate summation stage.

A finer table of lines.

The central approximation trade-off is to spend more lookup entries in order to use a lower-degree polynomial. HRS uses 16 intervals and evaluates a quadratic in each. The discovered circuit uses 128 intervals and evaluates only a line in each: the larger lookup is cheaper than the additional reversible multiplication required by a quadratic.

Both constructions first write d2=2e​ud^{2}=2^{e}u, with mantissa 1≤u<21\leq u<2, so that

1d2=2−e/21u.\frac{1}{\sqrt{d^{2}}}=2^{-e/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}. (66)

A few flag qubits record the scale 2−e/22^{-e/2}. The parity of ee and the six leading bits of the mantissa select one of 128 lines, and the next six bits give a local coordinate. The remaining low bits are irrelevant within the error bound. The selected line therefore needs at most six controlled additions rather than a general multiplication, after which the circuit restores the scale and adds the result to kk. As in the HHL circuit, the coefficients are fitted to the exact integer computation.

The larger table is affordable because MBU of a lookup [64] removes it with 17 Toffolis, instead of the 126 that reversing it would take.

The worst-case error over all attainable squared distances is 1.91×10−61.91\times 10^{-6} in the inverse distance. The circuit uses 1,140 Toffolis and 142 qubits, for a T​QTQ-cost of 160,000. Relative to the tuned HRS baseline, this reduces the Toffoli count by 5.6×5.6\times, the qubit count by 1.8×1.8\times, and the T​QTQ-cost by 9.9×9.9\times.

III.3 Fixed-point Gaussian

The Gaussian e−x2e^{-x^{2}} enters chemistry simulation through on-the-fly evaluation of molecular basis functions [2] and Gaussian state preparation [65]. The input is a 39-bit two’s-complement integer XsX_{s} representing x=Xs/232x=X_{s}/2^{32}, and the promised domain is x∈[−8,8)x\in[-8,8). The circuit adds

f⁡(Xs)=𝚛𝚘𝚞𝚗𝚍⁡(232​e−x2)f(X_{s})=\mathtt{round}\!\bigl(2^{32}e^{-x^{2}}\bigr) (67)

to a 39-bit accumulator with error below 10−710^{-7}. The tuned HRS baseline first forms x2x^{2} and evaluates cubics over 32 intervals using general 40-bit arithmetic, for 24,000 Toffolis and 362 qubits.

The discovered circuit never forms x2x^{2}. It folds the input onto the nonnegative axis and approximates e−y2e^{-y^{2}} directly. For a negative two’s-complement input, forming |x||x| would complement the data bits and add one. The circuit omits that addition, so the complement, which needs only Clifford gates, instead represents y=|x|−2−32y=|x|-2^{-32}. This removes an entire carry chain, and the resulting one-unit offset lies within the error budget.

Pruned coefficient lookup.

Ten bits of yy directly select one of 1,024 equal intervals of width 2−72^{-7} that cover [0,8)[0,8), while the lower bits give the local coordinate. The Gaussian’s decay divides these intervals into three regimes: 455 require quadratics, the next 59 need only constants, and the remaining 510 return zero. A conventional QROM would nevertheless spend gates on every interval. The variable-spaced QROM of Sanders et al. [66] instead stops whenever an entire subtree shares one value. Pruning the constant and zero intervals reduces the lookup from 1,022 Toffolis to 495.

Direct quadratic accumulation.

On a quadratic interval, the lookup returns an intercept, slope, and curvature. A truncated product updates the slope register in place, after which the circuit adds the intercept and accumulates the final product directly into kk. Consequently, it never forms y2y^{2} or a completed product, and it needs no separate Gaussian-value register. The coefficients are again fitted to the exact integer computation.

After MBU, the freed coefficient qubits serve as carry ancillas for the later arithmetic [64]. Together with direct accumulation, this reuse lowers the peak qubit count from 362 in the baseline to 139.

The worst-case error over the full domain is 9.99×10−89.99\times 10^{-8}. The circuit uses 1,583 Toffolis and 139 qubits, for a T​QTQ-cost of 220,000. Relative to the tuned HRS baseline, this reduces the Toffoli count by 15×15\times, the qubit count by 2.6×2.6\times, and the T​QTQ-cost by 39×39\times.

Across the three tasks, these techniques reduce T​QTQ-cost by 9.9×9.9\times–39×39\times relative to the tuned HRS baselines.

IV Quantum chemistry simulation

In Pauli-based electronic-structure simulation, the electronic Hamiltonian is a weighted sum of Pauli operators:

H=∑ℓ=0L−1wℓ​Pℓ,H=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}w_{\ell}P_{\ell}, (68)

where each PℓP_{\ell} is a tensor product of II, XX, YY, and ZZ. Qubitization encodes this Hamiltonian in a unitary circuit. Such an encoding is needed because HH is not itself unitary and therefore cannot simply be applied to a quantum state. Writing λ=∑ℓ|wℓ|\lambda=\sum_{\ell}|w_{\ell}|, an ideal Prepare creates a superposition of term labels,

Prepare​|0⟩=∑ℓ|wℓ|/λ​|ℓ⟩,\textsc{Prepare}\ket{0}=\sum_{\ell}\sqrt{|w_{\ell}|/\lambda}\ket{\ell}, (69)

while Select applies the signed Pauli operator with that label:

Select​|ℓ⟩​|ψ⟩=|ℓ⟩​sgn⁡(wℓ)​Pℓ​|ψ⟩.\textsc{Select}\ket{\ell}\ket{\psi}=\ket{\ell}\operatorname{sgn}(w_{\ell})P_{\ell}\ket{\psi}. (70)

Preparing this superposition, applying the selected term, and reversing the preparation embeds the normalized Hamiltonian as a block of a larger unitary:

(⟨0|⊗I)​Prepare†​SelectPrepare​(|0⟩⊗I)=∑ℓwℓλ​Pℓ=Hλ.(\bra{0}\otimes I)\textsc{Prepare}^{\dagger}\textsc{Select}\textsc{Prepare}(\ket{0}\otimes I)=\sum_{\ell}\frac{w_{\ell}}{\lambda}P_{\ell}=\frac{H}{\lambda}. (71)

Qubitization combines this block encoding with a reflection about the prepared state to form a quantum walk operator UU with eigenvalues e±i​arccos⁡(E/λ)e^{\pm i\arccos(E/\lambda)}, where EE ranges over the eigenenergies of HH. Phase estimation on UU therefore yields the energies; because it applies UU many times, the cost of one application sets the cost of the simulation.

We use the Fe2​S2\mathrm{Fe_{2}S_{2}} integral data published by Li and Chan [67], which models 30 active electrons in 20 spatial orbitals. Iron–sulfur clusters are important strongly correlated targets, in which many electronic configurations contribute significantly to the ground state [68, 69]. Each spatial orbital has a spin-up and a spin-down mode, so these 20 orbitals become 40 spin-orbitals and, after the Jordan–Wigner mapping, 40 qubits. Discarding terms with |wℓ|<10−4|w_{\ell}|<10^{-4} Ha, following the truncation practice of sparse qubitization [64], leaves L=41,052L=41{,}052 signed Pauli operators.

State-of-the-art resource estimates for this system use double-factorized tensor hypercontraction (DFTHC), which compresses the Hamiltonian into factors and orbital rotations before circuit construction [69]. However, studying the DFTHC walk operator would require validating networks of continuously parameterized Givens rotations acting on superposed states, which goes beyond the kickmix framework. We therefore focus on the more direct sparse compilation, which stores the Hamiltonian as an explicit list of its Pauli terms.

In this section we study the data-dependent part of one application of UU: the alias selection inside Prepare, the Select application, and the erasure of the selection. Directly preparing the unequal amplitudes in Equation 69 is expensive, so a standard construction uses the alias method [70, 71, 4, 64]. Classical preprocessing spreads the probabilities |wℓ|/λ|w_{\ell}|/\lambda over LL equal-sized buckets, one per term. Bucket ii is shared between term ii and one other term alt⁡(i)\operatorname{alt}(i), and a 16-bit threshold keep⁡(i)\operatorname{keep}(i) sets the split. The circuit draws a bucket ii and a 16-bit value τ\tau uniformly. It selects term ii if τ<keep⁡(i)\tau<\operatorname{keep}(i) and term alt⁡(i)\operatorname{alt}(i) otherwise:

h(i,τ)=𝟏[τ<keep(i)],sel(i,τ)={ifor ​h=1,alt⁡(i)for ​h=0.h(i,\tau)=\mathbf{1}[\tau<\operatorname{keep}(i)],\qquad\operatorname{sel}(i,\tau)=\begin{cases}i&\text{for }h=1,\\ \operatorname{alt}(i)&\text{for }h=0.\end{cases} (72)

The preprocessing chooses the alternate terms and thresholds so that, across all pairs (i,τ)(i,\tau), each term ℓ\ell is selected a number of times proportional to its weight, rounded to 16 bits. Thus choosing ii and τ\tau uniformly produces the rounded distribution. Let UaliasU_{\mathrm{alias}} denote the reversible computation of hh and sel\operatorname{sel} from ii and τ\tau. The data-dependent circuit studied here is Ualias†​Select​UaliasU_{\mathrm{alias}}^{\dagger}\textsc{Select}U_{\mathrm{alias}}: it computes the selected term, applies its signed Pauli operator, and erases the selection, leaving ii and τ\tau unchanged. The uniform-superposition preparation of ii and τ\tau, its reversal, and the walk reflection lie outside this circuit.

Each table row stores its threshold, its alternate index, and the signs of both possible coefficients. We call this 34-bit record the alias word. Write θℓ=0\theta_{\ell}=0 for a positive coefficient and θℓ=1\theta_{\ell}=1 for a negative one.

To state the required action on the system register xx, observe that on a computational-basis state, XX flips a bit, ZZ contributes a sign determined by that bit, and YY does both. For term ℓ\ell, let aℓa_{\ell} mark the qubits on which PℓP_{\ell} contains XX or YY, and let zℓz_{\ell} mark those on which it contains ZZ or YY. Write nY​(Pℓ)n_{Y}(P_{\ell}) for the number of YY factors in PℓP_{\ell}. Every Pauli operator in the table contains an even number of YY factors, so its phase is real:

Pℓ​|x⟩=(−1)ηℓ⊕parity⁡(x∧zℓ)​|x⊕aℓ⟩,ηℓ=nY​(Pℓ)mod42.P_{\ell}\ket{x}=(-1)^{\eta_{\ell}\oplus\operatorname{parity}(x\mathbin{\wedge}z_{\ell})}\ket{x\oplus a_{\ell}},\qquad\eta_{\ell}=\frac{n_{Y}(P_{\ell})\bmod 4}{2}. (73)

The required map is therefore

|i⟩16​|τ⟩16​|x⟩40⟼(−1)ϕ​|i⟩16​|τ⟩16​|x⊕asel⟩40,\ket{i}_{16}\ket{\tau}_{16}\ket{x}_{40}\longmapsto(-1)^{\phi}\ket{i}_{16}\ket{\tau}_{16}\ket{x\oplus a_{\operatorname{sel}}}_{40}, (74)

where

ϕ=θsel⊕ηsel⊕parity⁡(x∧zsel).\phi=\theta_{\operatorname{sel}}\oplus\eta_{\operatorname{sel}}\oplus\operatorname{parity}(x\mathbin{\wedge}z_{\operatorname{sel}}). (75)

The comparison bit hh and the selected index do not appear in this map: they are intermediate values that the circuit must return to zero. We require this map exactly for every i<41,052i<41{,}052, every τ\tau, and every 40-bit system state.

The baseline combines the circuits used in sparse qubitization [4, 64]. QROM loads the 34-bit alias word, merging repeated alias words [66]. A comparator then calculates h⁡(i,τ)h(i,\tau) to choose between ii and alt⁡(i)\operatorname{alt}(i) and apply the selected coefficient sign. A second, independent traversal over sel\operatorname{sel} applies the selected Pauli operator to the 40 system qubits. The baseline then erases the selected index, the comparison bit hh, and the alias word.

The lookup and the row-by-row Select traversal cost 13,000 and 41,000 Toffolis, respectively; together they contribute more than 97%97\% of the total. The remaining comparison, selection, and cleanup bring the baseline to 55,000 Toffolis and 139 qubits. The main opportunity is to shorten the two table traversals.

For arbitrary, unstructured table data, QROM has no pattern to exploit: in the worst case, every address may store an unrelated word. However, this table is not arbitrary. Its Pauli operators and coefficients come from a physical system with exact spin symmetries and repeated orbital environments, so many coefficients are equal and many Pauli operators are related. We therefore choose the table to suit the circuits. Two degrees of freedom make this possible. First, permuting terms together with their coefficients and Pauli operators leaves Equation 68 unchanged. Second, many different alias tables realize the same rounded distribution. The preprocessing uses the first freedom to group Pauli operators related by fixed Clifford transformations into blocks, shortening Select. It uses the second to place equal alias words into repeated patterns, shortening QROM.

Frame-block Select.

Many Pauli operators in this Hamiltonian are related by fixed Clifford transformations, which we call frames. Suppose, for example, that two commuting frames generate four related Pauli operators from one representative. Instead of selecting four operators independently, the circuit selects the representative once and uses two bits of the address (the selected row index) to control the two frames. More generally, kk such bits can identify up to 2k2^{k} operators in a block. The circuit pays for one block representative plus its controlled frames, rather than every Pauli operator separately.

The circuit applies a frame by conjugation. It applies σ†\sigma^{\dagger} to the system register under a control, then the representative PP, then σ\sigma under the same control. The result is σ​P​σ†\sigma P\sigma^{\dagger} when the control is set and PP otherwise. Each frame is applied once for the whole table rather than once per block. Blocks that use the same frames are contiguous, so a few comparisons of the address with fixed boundaries determine which frames are active.

These relations have a physical origin: the model contains two equivalent spin channels, two similar iron sites, and corresponding orbitals on repeated parts of the cluster. These repetitions create Pauli operators that are related by a fixed transformation. Each frame is a permutation or change of basis of the spin-orbitals. The Jordan–Wigner mapping turns it into a fixed Clifford transformation of the 40 system qubits.

Two of the frames used here come from exact spin symmetries of the Hamiltonian. Because the model treats the spin-up and spin-down channels identically, σα​β\sigma_{\alpha\beta} exchanges the spin-up and spin-down modes of every spatial orbital. Spin-rotation symmetry produces a second pairing after the Jordan–Wigner mapping: σX​Y\sigma_{XY} exchanges the XX and YY factors and adjusts the accompanying ZZ strings required by that mapping. Both transformations preserve the corresponding coefficient magnitudes.

The other five frames come from parts of the cluster that resemble each other; unlike the two spin frames, they are not symmetries of the full Hamiltonian. The frame σFe\sigma_{\mathrm{Fe}} is the approximate left–right reflection of the cluster, which exchanges the two iron centers and their surrounding orbitals. The frame σFe′\sigma^{\prime}_{\mathrm{Fe}} combines this reflection with several local orbital swaps and matches Pauli operators that the bare reflection misses. The frames σthio\sigma_{\mathrm{thio}}, σ3​d\sigma_{3d}, and σμ​S\sigma_{\mu\mathrm{S}} exchange corresponding orbitals on the terminal thiolates, the iron 3​d3d shells, and the bridging sulfur atoms. These sites have similar but not identical electronic environments: the permutation often maps one term’s Pauli operator onto another’s, but the coefficients differ. Only the Pauli relation Pℓ′=σ​Pℓ​σ†P_{\ell^{\prime}}=\sigma P_{\ell}\sigma^{\dagger} must hold exactly; wℓ′w_{\ell^{\prime}} and wℓw_{\ell} remain independent entries in the alias table.

The preprocessing thus finds a commuting family of seven frames and orders related Pauli operators into blocks whose sizes are powers of two, so that address bits index the operators within a block. The 41,052 terms form 3,221 blocks. Selecting the block representatives costs 3,327 Toffolis. Applying the seven frames and determining which are active costs 534. Figure S4 shows the resulting structure.

Alias table with repeated rows.

Recall that each alias-table row is a probability bucket split between its own term and one alternate term. A term whose weight is smaller than one bucket leaves empty space in its row; a term whose weight is larger than one bucket fills such space in other rows.

A standard alias construction may pair underfilled rows with heavy terms in many different ways. Our preprocessing chooses these pairings to make nearby rows identical. For example, if four light rows of equal weight must draw their alternate terms from two heavy terms AA and BB, an ordinary schedule might alternate A,B,A,BA,B,A,B; ours prefers A,A,B,BA,A,B,B. Rows 1–2 then share a threshold, an alternate term, and hence an alias word, as do rows 3–4.

This strategy is particularly effective here because the two exact spin frames produce many groups of four equal weights (Figure S4(b)). The coefficients also span a broad range, so heavier terms can supply the missing weight of many lighter rows. Because the pairing only redistributes each term’s weight among buckets, it preserves the rounded distribution and creates long runs of identical alias words without breaking the frame blocks. Of the 20,374 σα​β\sigma_{\alpha\beta}-related row pairs it places next to each other, 18,463 store identical alias words.

The alias-table QROM realizes this saving by pruning the binary tree over its address ii. Whenever the two halves of a subtree contain the same sequence of alias words, the QROM visits one copy and skips the address bit that distinguishes them. For example, the eight-row pattern A,A,B,B,A,A,B,BA,A,B,B,A,A,B,B consists of two identical halves, so the top address bit is irrelevant and the circuit looks up only A,A,B,BA,A,B,B. Together, this scheduling and repeated-subtree pruning reduce the cost of the alias-table QROM to 10,000 Toffolis, compared with 41,000 for a row-by-row traversal and 13,000 for the baseline lookup with merged repeated alias words.

The rest of the circuit follows the baseline. A comparator computes hh, a controlled swap moves the selected index into place, and both are reversed after Select, for 64 Toffolis. The circuit then clears the keep\operatorname{keep} and alt\operatorname{alt} fields by MBU and corrects the resulting phase in one pass over the address ii, for 782 Toffolis.

We test every table row and a further 2242^{24} uniformly random inputs. The discovered circuit uses 15,000 Toffolis and 126 qubits, for a T​QTQ-cost of 1.9×1061.9\times 10^{6}. Relative to the baseline, this reduces the Toffoli count by 3.7×3.7\times, the qubit count by 9.4%9.4\%, and the T​QTQ-cost by 4.1×4.1\times.

The amount of compression is specific to this Hamiltonian, but the preprocessing can search for such relations in other sparse Pauli tables, and it falls back to conventional Select and QROM costs when it finds none. Exact spin symmetry is common in spin-independent molecular Hamiltonians, so the scheduling strategy should carry over. The opportunity is smaller when a Zeeman term or spin–orbit coupling breaks the spin symmetries. In DFTHC, analogous choices arise in the factorization itself [72, 69]: the factorization is not unique, and a circuit-aware choice could make its coefficient data repeated or sparse and therefore cheaper to load.

V Nonabelian lattice-gauge simulation

In Hamiltonian lattice gauge theory, space is replaced by a grid. A gauge-field configuration assigns a group element Ui​(𝐱)U_{i}(\mathbf{x}) to each directed edge, or link, from site 𝐱\mathbf{x} in direction ii. This element describes how the gauge field transports a state between neighboring sites; traversing the link backward contributes its inverse Ui​(𝐱)−1U_{i}(\mathbf{x})^{-1}. Multiplying the links around a closed path therefore describes the net transport along that loop. Although this product depends on an arbitrary convention at each site (the gauge), the real part of its matrix trace does not, and these loop traces form the magnetic energy [73]. Because the gauge group is nonabelian, its elements need not commute, so the links must be multiplied in the order in which the path traverses them.

We consider the group-register formulation of Hamiltonian lattice gauge theory [73], in which a register holds the group element of each link. The Hamiltonian separates into an electric (kinetic) term HEH_{E} and a magnetic (potential) term HBH_{B}. A Trotter step evolves these terms separately. Here we implement the magnetic evolution e−i​Δ​t​HBe^{-i\Delta tH_{B}} for the improved Hamiltonian of Carena et al. [74]. The smallest loop contributing to HBH_{B} goes around one square face of the lattice and is called a plaquette; the standard magnetic term sums a trace over these four-link loops. The improved Hamiltonian adds weighted 2×12\times 1 rectangles, which cancel the leading discretization error. Thus the magnetic evolution requires the same basic operation at many locations: follow a short closed path, multiply its links in order, extract a trace, and add the weighted result to the phase. The compilation task studied here is one application of the magnetic evolution to the whole lattice, which we call the magnetic layer.

We use a periodic 4×4×44\times 4\times 4 lattice 66 6 The resource estimate of Osorio Perez et al. [37] uses a 10310^{3} lattice. In this work, we use 434^{3} for ease of evaluation.. The lattice has 192 links, and the layer contains 192 four-link plaquettes and 384 six-link rectangles. For directions ii and jj, representative loop products are

Pi​j​(𝐱)=Ui​(𝐱)​Uj​(𝐱+i^)​Ui​(𝐱+j^)−1​Uj​(𝐱)−1,Ri​j​(𝐱)=Ui​(𝐱)​Ui​(𝐱+i^)​Uj​(𝐱+2​i^)​Ui​(𝐱+i^+j^)−1​Ui​(𝐱+j^)−1​Uj​(𝐱)−1.\begin{gathered}P_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=U_{i}(\mathbf{x})U_{j}(\mathbf{x}+\hat{i})U_{i}(\mathbf{x}+\hat{j})^{-1}U_{j}(\mathbf{x})^{-1},\\ R_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=U_{i}(\mathbf{x})U_{i}(\mathbf{x}+\hat{i})U_{j}(\mathbf{x}+2\hat{i})U_{i}(\mathbf{x}+\hat{i}+\hat{j})^{-1}U_{i}(\mathbf{x}+\hat{j})^{-1}U_{j}(\mathbf{x})^{-1}.\end{gathered} (76)

Here i^\hat{i} is one lattice step in direction ii, with coordinates wrapping modulo four. Plaquettes use the pairs i<ji<j, and rectangles use both orderings i≠ji\neq j.

To store each link in a finite register, we restrict its value from the continuous group S​U​(3)SU(3) to the 216-element subgroup G=Σ⁡(72×3)⊂S​U​(3)G=\Sigma(72\times 3)\subset SU(3) used by Osorio Perez et al. [37]. We encode these elements using the unique normal form

g=ωp​Cq​Er​V2​s+t​Xu,p,q,r∈{0,1,2},s,t,u∈{0,1},g=\omega^{p}C^{q}E^{r}V^{2s+t}X^{u},\qquad p,q,r\in\{0,1,2\},\qquad s,t,u\in\{0,1\}, (77)

where ω=e2​π​i/3\omega=e^{2\pi i/3} and C,E,V,XC,E,V,X are fixed matrices that generate the group. These six exponents are the coordinates of a group element. Each three-valued exponent uses two qubits and each binary exponent one, for nine qubits per link and 1,728 in total. We write gg for the value of one link and g0,…,g191g_{0},\ldots,g_{191} for all of them. Setting u=0u=0 in Equation 77 gives the 108-element subgroup Σ⁡(36×3)\Sigma(36\times 3), while u=1u=1 gives its other coset.

The main difficulty in multiplying two group elements is that the generators do not commute. For instance, within the ω,C,E\omega,C,E part, the relation E​C=ω​C​EEC=\omega CE gives

(ωP​CQ​ER)​(ωp​Cq​Er)=ωP+p+R​q​CQ+q​ER+r,(\omega^{P}C^{Q}E^{R})(\omega^{p}C^{q}E^{r})=\omega^{P+p+Rq}C^{Q+q}E^{R+r}, (78)

with exponents modulo three. Moving VV through the C,EC,E part similarly transforms several coordinates. The action of XX is more involved:

X​C=C2​E​X,X​E=ω2​C​E​X,X​V=ω2​E​V3​X,X2=C2​V2.XC=C^{2}EX,\qquad XE=\omega^{2}CEX,\qquad XV=\omega^{2}EV^{3}X,\qquad X^{2}=C^{2}V^{2}. (79)

Consequently, when the left factor contains XX, every coordinate of the right factor must be rewritten before the two can be combined. Section V(a) gives the general rule.

Each g∈Gg\in G can be written as a 3×33\times 3 matrix MgM_{g}, and each completed loop product contributes to HBH_{B} only through the seven-valued function

f⁡(g)=2​Re⁡Tr⁡(Mg)∈{−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,6}.f(g)=2\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(M_{g})\in\{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,6\}. (80)

Let SPS_{P} and SRS_{R} be the sums of ff over all plaquettes and rectangles, respectively. For the improved discretization, HBH_{B} is proportional to SP−120​SRS_{P}-\frac{1}{20}S_{R} [74]. We represent these phase weights as 51-bit integers aPa_{P} and aRa_{R}. The weight aPa_{P} depends on the time step and the coupling, so we use a generic 51-bit value, and we choose aRa_{R} so that aR/aP≈−1/20a_{R}/a_{P}\approx-1/20. Because all of the loop traces are diagonal in the group-element basis, the magnetic evolution leaves each link configuration unchanged. In our 51-bit representation, the target operation multiplies each link configuration by the phase e2​π​i​(aP​SP+aR​SR)/251e^{2\pi i(a_{P}S_{P}+a_{R}S_{R})/2^{51}}. We implement this operation using a reusable phase-gradient state, which satisfies

|PG51⟩=1251∑k=0251−1e−2πik/251|k⟩,ADDy|PG51⟩=e2​π​i​y/251|PG51⟩,\ket{\mathrm{PG}_{51}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{51}}}\sum_{k=0}^{2^{51}-1}e^{-2\pi ik/2^{51}}\ket{k},\qquad\operatorname{ADD}_{y}\ket{\mathrm{PG}_{51}}=e^{2\pi iy/2^{51}}\ket{\mathrm{PG}_{51}}, (81)

where ADDy\operatorname{ADD}_{y} denotes modular addition by yy. Taking y=aP​SP+aR​SRy=a_{P}S_{P}+a_{R}S_{R} therefore applies the desired phase to the link registers while leaving the phase-gradient state unchanged. This reduces the compilation task to constructing the underlying reversible addition

|g0⋯g191⟩​|k⟩⟼|g0⋯g191⟩​|k+aP​SP+aR​SRmod251⟩,\ket{g_{0}\cdots g_{191}}\ket{k}\longmapsto\ket{g_{0}\cdots g_{191}}\ket{k+a_{P}S_{P}+a_{R}S_{R}\bmod 2^{51}}, (82)

for arbitrary computational-basis values kk.

The baseline treats all 576 loops independently, combining the inversion and multiplication circuits of Osorio Perez et al. [37], whose inner Σ⁡(36×3)\Sigma(36\times 3) circuits come from Gustafson et al. [76]; we implement these circuits from the published descriptions. For a loop LL, let a⁡(L)=aPa(L)=a_{P} for a plaquette and a⁡(L)=aRa(L)=a_{R} for a rectangle. For each loop, the baseline starts with W=1W=1 and successively multiplies the four or six directed links into it, so WW is the running product of the links traversed so far. After completing the loop, the baseline looks up the 51-bit addend a⁡(L)​f​(W)a(L)f(W) by QROM [4], adds it to kk, and reverses the lookup and loop product. Each multiplication costs 146 Toffolis and each link inversion costs 87. A plaquette costs 1,702 Toffolis and a rectangle costs 2,460, so the 192 plaquettes and 384 rectangles cost 1.3 million Toffolis. The baseline peaks at 1,927 qubits.
