The discovered circuit combines three optimizations. First, it uses different factor orders for the links and the running product, which makes updates of WW cheap. Second, it reuses partial loop products across the layer instead of computing every loop from the identity. Third, it avoids QROM by reading the trace value directly from the coordinates of WW and using the result to control the addition of a known constant.

Specialized running-product representation.

Repeatedly multiplying the running product WW by links dominates the cost, so the circuit uses a representation tailored to the restricted update W←W​gW\leftarrow Wg rather than to arbitrary group multiplication. Multiplication in the original normal form is costly in part because XX has a complicated conjugation action. However, the normal form can use any element of the u=1u=1 coset in place of XX. We replace XX by Xo=C​E​XX_{o}=CEX. Because XoX_{o} differs from XX only by factors of CC and EE, rewriting a link in terms of XoX_{o} changes only p,q,rp,q,r. XoX_{o} is the unique such element that satisfies

Xo​V​Xo−1=V−1,Xo2=V2.X_{o}VX_{o}^{-1}=V^{-1},\qquad X_{o}^{2}=V^{2}. (83)

Compare these relations with Equation 79: the V,XoV,X_{o} part now closes on itself instead of spilling corrections into the other coordinates.

After making this replacement, the circuit uses different factor orders for the links and for WW. Each link is recoded as

g=ωp​Cq​Er​Vm​Xou,g=\omega^{p}C^{q}E^{r}V^{m}X_{o}^{u}, (84)

whereas the frequently updated product is stored in the opposite order,

W=ωP​VM​Xoυ​CQ​ER,W=\omega^{P}V^{M}X_{o}^{\upsilon}C^{Q}E^{R}, (85)

with p,q,r,P,Q,R∈ℤ3p,q,r,P,Q,R\in\mathbb{Z}_{3}, m,M∈ℤ4m,M\in\mathbb{Z}_{4}, and u,υ∈ℤ2u,\upsilon\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}. This places the incoming and accumulated C,EC,E factors next to one another in W​gWg, so they can be combined directly before a few fixed permutations account for the remaining factors. One complication remains: reordering the factors would ordinarily introduce recurring corrections to the coordinate PP. The circuit stores P~=P+Q​R(mod3)\widetilde{P}=P+QR\pmod{3}, folding those corrections into the coordinate itself rather than recomputing them during every multiplication.

The 192 links are recoded once before the first loop and restored after the last. Each recoded link remains in a compact nine-qubit encoding; storing every link one-hot would cost three additional qubits per link. In contrast, there is only one running product, so we can afford to store its three-valued coordinates P~\widetilde{P}, QQ, and RR one-hot (three qubits, exactly one set), increasing the size of WW from nine to twelve qubits. Adding one modulo three then becomes a cyclic permutation of three qubits, while negation becomes a single swap. Controlled additions and the fixed transformations above can therefore use controlled qubit permutations rather than arithmetic on the two-qubit encoding. Together, these representation choices reduce each update of WW from 146 Toffolis in the baseline’s general multiplication circuit to 35 Toffolis. Multiplying by an inverse link g−1g^{-1} costs the same, so the circuit needs no separate link inversion. Section V gives the complete coordinate rules for both representations.

Reusing loop products.

The baseline constructs each loop product from the identity and then reverses the construction. Neighboring loops, however, often share a sequence of factors. The discovered circuit therefore retains WW after one trace evaluation and edits it into the product needed for the next, reusing the shared factors instead of rebuilding them.

More loops share factors than first appears, because the real trace is invariant under cyclic rotation and inversion:

f(h1h2⋯hn)=f(h2⋯hnh1)=f((h1h2⋯hn)−1).f(h_{1}h_{2}\cdots h_{n})=f(h_{2}\cdots h_{n}h_{1})=f((h_{1}h_{2}\cdots h_{n})^{-1}). (86)

The first equality is cyclicity of the matrix trace; the second follows because these matrices are unitary and ff takes the real part. For example, to change a​b​c​d​eabcde into a​b​c​x​yabcxy, the circuit right-multiplies by e−1e^{-1} and d−1d^{-1} to cancel the old suffix, then appends xx and yy, retaining the common prefix a​b​cabc. Inverting WW, which costs 21 Toffolis, makes the other end of the product available for the same operation. Cyclic rotations and inversion also give several equivalent ways to write each loop, which we call its representatives, all with the same value of ff. As Figure S5(a) illustrates, a good choice can expose a longer segment shared with the next loop. A classical dynamic program chooses the representatives and the order in which the loops are evaluated, minimizing the cost of transforming WW between consecutive representatives. The chosen schedule uses 3,136 link multiplications and 480 inversions of WW for the 576 loops, about 5.4 multiplications per loop. By comparison, building and reversing each loop separately takes 6 multiplications for a plaquette and 10 for a rectangle.

Reading the trace directly.

The baseline in Figure S5(b) uses WW as the address of a 216-entry QROM and loads a full 51-bit addend, although f⁡(W)f(W) has only seven possible values. The discovered circuit instead computes which of the seven values occurs. In the specialized representation, a small Boolean circuit acting directly on (P~,M,υ,Q,R)(\widetilde{P},M,\upsilon,Q,R) computes six flag qubits, one per nonzero trace value, of which at most one is set (Figure S5(c)). Each flag controls the addition of the corresponding constant a⁡(L)​va(L)v to kk, where vv is the flagged trace value, so the circuit never stores a 51-bit lookup result. Computing the six flags costs 20 Toffolis. Readout, addition, and cleanup cost 76 Toffolis for a plaquette and 75 for a rectangle, compared with 478 for the baseline QROM lookup, addition, and unlookup.

We test the complete circuit on 100,000 random inputs and each group operation on all of its inputs. The discovered circuit uses 170,000 Toffolis and 1,859 qubits, for a T​QTQ-cost of 3.2×1083.2\times 10^{8}. Relative to the baseline, this reduces the Toffoli count by 7.4×7.4\times, the qubit count by 3.5%3.5\%, and the T​QTQ-cost by 7.7×7.7\times. Updates of WW account for 110,000 of the Toffolis, trace readout and addition for 43,000, inversions of WW for 10,000, and link recoding for 8,832.

Appendix

Appendix A Exact branch recovery for divstep inversion

This appendix proves the decoding rule of Equation 9 [16]. The argument first establishes the invariants carried by the coefficients fvf_{v} and gvg_{v}, then identifies the decisions already visible from the updated state, and finally shows how the remaining bit bb is encoded in a window of low-order bits. Let pp be an odd positive integer and let 0≤w<p0\leq w<p. The walk begins at

(z,f,g,fv,gv)=(0,p,w,0,1).(z,f,g,f_{v},g_{v})=(0,p,w,0,1). (A1)

Every step follows the recurrence

(z′,f′,g′,fv′,gv′)={(−z,g,(g−f)/2, 2​gv,gv−fv)for ​z≥0,g​ odd,(z+1,f,(g+f)/2, 2​fv,gv+fv)for ​z<0,g​ odd,(z+1,f,g/2, 2​fv,gv)for ​g​ even.(z^{\prime},f^{\prime},g^{\prime},f_{v}^{\prime},g_{v}^{\prime})=\begin{cases}(-z,\ g,\ (g-f)/2,\ 2g_{v},\ g_{v}-f_{v})&\text{for }z\geq 0,\ g\text{ odd},\\ (z+1,\ f,\ (g+f)/2,\ 2f_{v},\ g_{v}+f_{v})&\text{for }z<0,\ g\text{ odd},\\ (z+1,\ f,\ g/2,\ 2f_{v},\ g_{v})&\text{for }g\text{ even}.\end{cases} (A2)

Let ss indicate whether the step swaps, and let b=1b=1 exactly when gg is odd, so bb records whether the two values are combined before halving. In this notation, s=1s=1 selects the first case of Equation A2; when s=0s=0, the value of bb selects the second or third case. The walk freezes when gg first becomes zero; the steps before that are active.

For an integer uu and k≥0k\geq 0, write u⁡[k]∈{0,1}u[k]\in\{0,1\} for bit kk of umod2k+1u\bmod 2^{k+1}, counted from zero. This notation agrees with the usual binary digit for u≥0u\geq 0 and with the two’s-complement digit for u<0u<0. We also write bitk⁡(u)=u⁡[k]\operatorname{bit}_{k}(u)=u[k]. Let v2​(u)v_{2}(u) denote the number of trailing zero bits of uu (its 22-adic valuation), with v2​(0)=+∞v_{2}(0)=+\infty.

We first show, via the determinant and scaling relations, that the integer recurrence computes a modular inverse.

Lemma A.1 (Basic invariants).

Every reachable state satisfies

f​gv−g​fv=p.fg_{v}-gf_{v}=p. (A3)

Moreover, ff and gvg_{v} are odd and fvf_{v} is even.

Proof.

The initial state gives p⋅1−w⋅0=pp\cdot 1-w\cdot 0=p. Direct substitution in the nonswap and swap cases gives

f⁡(gv+b​fv)−g+b​f2​(2​fv)\displaystyle f(g_{v}+bf_{v})-\frac{g+bf}{2}(2f_{v}) =f​gv−g​fv,\displaystyle=fg_{v}-gf_{v}, (nonswap),\displaystyle\text{(nonswap)}, (A4)
g⁡(gv−fv)−g−f2​(2​gv)\displaystyle g(g_{v}-f_{v})-\frac{g-f}{2}(2g_{v}) =f​gv−g​fv,\displaystyle=fg_{v}-gf_{v}, (swap).\displaystyle\text{(swap)}.

Hence every active step preserves the determinant, while a frozen step leaves the state unchanged. The parity claims also hold at the initial state. On a nonswap, ff remains odd, fv′=2​fvf_{v}^{\prime}=2f_{v} is even, and gv′=gv+b​fvg_{v}^{\prime}=g_{v}+bf_{v} is odd. On a swap, the swap condition (gg odd) makes f′=gf^{\prime}=g odd, while fv′=2​gvf_{v}^{\prime}=2g_{v} is even and gv′=gv−fvg_{v}^{\prime}=g_{v}-f_{v} is odd. Induction proves all four claims. ∎

Proposition A.2 (Scaling and termination).

After tt active steps,

fv​w≡2t​f(modp),gv​w≡2t​g(modp).f_{v}w\equiv 2^{t}f\pmod{p},\qquad g_{v}w\equiv 2^{t}g\pmod{p}. (A5)

If gcd⁡(p,w)=1\gcd(p,w)=1, then at termination f=±1f=\pm 1, gv=f​pg_{v}=fp, and

w−1≡f​fv​2−t(modp).w^{-1}\equiv ff_{v}2^{-t}\pmod{p}. (A6)
Proof.

The congruences hold at the initial state. Substitution in Equation A2 shows that if they hold after tt active steps, the updated coefficients satisfy them with t+1t+1 in place of tt. They therefore hold for every tt. Every step also preserves gcd⁡(f,g)\gcd(f,g), so termination with g=0g=0 gives |f|=gcd⁡(p,w)=1|f|=\gcd(p,w)=1. The determinant invariant then gives gv=f​pg_{v}=fp, and multiplying the first congruence by ff yields Equation A6. ∎

Before turning to the decoding rule, we record the independent worst-case termination guarantee used by the circuit analysis.

Proposition A.3 (Worst-case step bound).

Let p=2256−232−977p=2^{256}-2^{32}-977. For every 0≤w<p0\leq w<p, the walk in Equation A1 reaches g=0g=0 within 590590 active steps. If w>0w>0, its final coefficients satisfy Equation A6; if w=0w=0, the walk starts frozen.

Proof.

The worst-case analysis of Wuille [36] guarantees that every 0<w<p0<w<p reaches g=0g=0 within 590590 divsteps. The case w=0w=0 starts with g=0g=0. For 0<w<p0<w<p, gcd⁡(p,w)=1\gcd(p,w)=1 because pp is prime, so once the walk terminates, the remaining claims follow from Proposition A.2. ∎

We now recover the bits ss and bb of an active step from its updated state. The bit ss, and bb in two special cases, can be read from a few bits of that state.

Lemma A.4 (Locally visible decisions).

Every active step has the following properties:

  1. 1.

    The swap is visible from the updated coefficient:

    s=1⟺fv′≡2(mod4)⟺v2(fv′)=1.s=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f_{v}^{\prime}\equiv 2\pmod{4}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v_{2}(f_{v}^{\prime})=1. (A7)

    If s=0s=0, then 4|fv′4\mid f_{v}^{\prime}; moreover, s=1s=1 implies b=1b=1.

  2. 2.

    If s=0s=0 and z′≥1z^{\prime}\geq 1, then b=0b=0.

  3. 3.

    If g′=0g^{\prime}=0, then b=1b=1.

Proof.

On a swap step, the incoming gg is odd, so b=1b=1; the update also gives f′=gf^{\prime}=g, preserving the oddness of ff. Moreover, fv′=2​gvf_{v}^{\prime}=2g_{v}, which is twice an odd integer by Lemma A.1. On a nonswap step, fv′=2​fvf_{v}^{\prime}=2f_{v}, which is divisible by four. This proves part 1. For part 2, a nonswap has z=z′−1≥0z=z^{\prime}-1\geq 0. Since the swap condition nevertheless failed, the incoming value gg was even, and hence b=0b=0. Finally, on a nonswap, g′=(g+b​f)/2g^{\prime}=(g+bf)/2. If b=0b=0 and g′=0g^{\prime}=0, then g=0g=0, contrary to the step being active; a swap already has b=1b=1 by part 1. This proves part 3. ∎

The steps these tests leave undecided, apart from a terminating step, are the nonswaps entered with z<0z<0; we call them negative-counter nonswaps. Their decisions are the ambiguous decisions of SI II.1: the preceding tests do not determine bb, but the coefficients still retain it. Whenever fv≠0f_{v}\neq 0, put j=v2​(fv)j=v_{2}(f_{v}) and write fv=2j​qf_{v}=2^{j}q with qq odd. On an updated state, jj is the excursion depth defined in the main text, and a swap followed by a run of ambiguous decisions is an excursion. The jj low-order bits of gv​q−1g_{v}q^{-1}, which we call the window, accumulate successive decisions.

Lemma A.5 (Window invariant).

Every reachable state satisfies the following conditions:

  1. 1.

    If z≥0z\geq 0, then 2z+1|fv2^{z+1}\mid f_{v}.

  2. 2.

    If z<0z<0, then fv≠0f_{v}\neq 0 and, with j=v2​(fv)j=v_{2}(f_{v}) and q=fv/2jq=f_{v}/2^{j}, there is an integer cc such that 0≤c<2j0\leq c<2^{j} and

    gv≡q​c(mod2j−z).g_{v}\equiv qc\pmod{2^{j-z}}. (A8)

Because qq is odd, part 2 says that gv​q−1mod2j−zg_{v}q^{-1}\bmod 2^{j-z} fits in jj bits: the −z-z bits above position j−1j-1 vanish.

Proof.

Proceed by induction along the walk. A frozen step changes nothing. At the initial state, z=0z=0, fv=0f_{v}=0, and 2|fv2\mid f_{v}.

Suppose first that a nonswap begins with z≥0z\geq 0. Then z′=z+1z^{\prime}=z+1 and fv′=2​fvf_{v}^{\prime}=2f_{v}, so 2z′+1|fv′2^{z^{\prime}+1}\mid f_{v}^{\prime}.

Suppose next that a swap occurs at z=D≥0z=D\geq 0. Then z′=−Dz^{\prime}=-D and fv′=2​gvf_{v}^{\prime}=2g_{v}. By Lemma A.1, gvg_{v} is odd, so v2​(fv′)=1v_{2}(f_{v}^{\prime})=1 and the odd part of fv′f_{v}^{\prime} is gvg_{v}. Moreover, gv′=gv−fvg_{v}^{\prime}=g_{v}-f_{v}, while the induction hypothesis gives 2D+1|fv2^{D+1}\mid f_{v}. Hence

gv′≡gv(mod2D+1).g_{v}^{\prime}\equiv g_{v}\pmod{2^{D+1}}. (A9)

If D>0D>0, part 2 holds with j=1j=1 and c=1c=1; if D=0D=0, part 1 asks only that 2|fv′2\mid f_{v}^{\prime}.

Finally, suppose that a nonswap begins with z<0z<0. Let j=v2​(fv)j=v_{2}(f_{v}) and let cc be the witness from part 2. Then z′=z+1z^{\prime}=z+1, fv′=2​fvf_{v}^{\prime}=2f_{v}, and the odd part qq is unchanged. Since gv′=gv+b​fvg_{v}^{\prime}=g_{v}+bf_{v},

gv′≡q⁡(c+b​2j)(mod2j−z),0≤c+b​2j<2j+1.g_{v}^{\prime}\equiv q(c+b2^{j})\pmod{2^{j-z}},\qquad 0\leq c+b2^{j}<2^{j+1}. (A10)

The invariant makes the bit bb of every negative-counter nonswap an exact function of the updated state.

Theorem A.6 (Decoding rule for an ambiguous decision).

Let (z′,f′,g′,fv′,gv′)(z^{\prime},f^{\prime},g^{\prime},f_{v}^{\prime},g_{v}^{\prime}) be the updated state of a negative-counter nonswap. Put j=v2​(fv′)j=v_{2}(f_{v}^{\prime}) and q=fv′/2jq=f_{v}^{\prime}/2^{j}. Then j≥2j\geq 2, qq is odd, and

b=bitj−1⁡(gv′​q−1mod2j)=bitj−1⁡(p​(f′​q)−1mod2j).b=\operatorname{bit}_{j-1}\!\left(g_{v}^{\prime}q^{-1}\bmod 2^{j}\right)=\operatorname{bit}_{j-1}\!\left(p(f^{\prime}q)^{-1}\bmod 2^{j}\right). (A11)

In particular, for fixed odd pp, the bit bb is determined by (j,f′mod2j,qmod2j)(j,f^{\prime}\bmod 2^{j},q\bmod 2^{j}).

Proof.

The step doubles fvf_{v}, so its incoming valuation is j−1j-1. The window invariant makes the incoming fvf_{v} nonzero, while Lemma A.1 makes it even; hence j≥2j\geq 2. By definition, qq is odd. The modulus provided by part 2 of Lemma A.5 is 2(j−1)−z2^{(j-1)-z}, which is divisible by 2j2^{j}. The invariant therefore supplies a cc with 0≤c<2j−10\leq c<2^{j-1} and gv≡q​c(mod2j)g_{v}\equiv qc\pmod{2^{j}}. The odd part qq is unchanged, and the update gives

gv′≡q⁡(c+b​2j−1)(mod2j).g_{v}^{\prime}\equiv q(c+b2^{j-1})\pmod{2^{j}}. (A12)

Since qq is odd and 0≤c+b​2j−1<2j0\leq c+b2^{j-1}<2^{j}, bit j−1j-1 of gv′​q−1mod2jg_{v}^{\prime}q^{-1}\bmod 2^{j} is exactly bb. For the second form, reduce the determinant identity f′​gv′−g′​fv′=pf^{\prime}g_{v}^{\prime}-g^{\prime}f_{v}^{\prime}=p modulo 2j2^{j}. Because 2j|fv′2^{j}\mid f_{v}^{\prime} and f′f^{\prime} is odd, gv′≡p​(f′)−1(mod2j)g_{v}^{\prime}\equiv p(f^{\prime})^{-1}\pmod{2^{j}}. Substitution into the first form gives the second. ∎

The proof also shows how the window records the decisions. Immediately after the swap that begins an excursion, the window contains 11; each subsequent negative-counter nonswap places its bit bb in the next higher position. Thus, at depth jj, the window contains

1+∑k=1j−1bk​2k,1+\sum_{k=1}^{j-1}b_{k}2^{k}, (A13)

where bkb_{k} is the bit bb of the kkth negative-counter nonswap after the swap.

Corollary A.7 (Finite dependence).

For each fixed odd pp, the bit bb at depth jj is determined by at most 2​j2j bits of the updated state.

Proof.

By Theorem A.6, the residues of f′f^{\prime} and qq modulo 2j2^{j} determine bb, and each residue is represented by jj bits. ∎

Corollary A.8 (Depth-two rule).

At every negative-counter nonswap with j=2j=2,

b=gv′​[1]⊕fv′​[3].b=g_{v}^{\prime}[1]\mathbin{\oplus}f_{v}^{\prime}[3]. (A14)
Proof.

By Theorem A.6, b=bit1⁡(gv′​q−1mod4)b=\operatorname{bit}_{1}(g_{v}^{\prime}q^{-1}\bmod 4) with q=fv′/4q=f_{v}^{\prime}/4. Every odd qq satisfies q−1≡q(mod4)q^{-1}\equiv q\pmod{4}.
